items.content:
Strait of Hormuz attacks have increased to highest level since Iran war began
The attacks could complicate U.S.-led efforts to keep oil flowing.
Reported attacks in and around the Strait of Hormuz have been higher in number in October and November than any previous months since the war between the U.S., Israel and Iran began in late February , according to data compiled by maritime organizations.
The attacks appear to be a bid to complicate U.S.-led efforts to keep oil flowing through the economically crucial Strait of Hormuz despite an Iranian-declared blockade, experts told ABC News.
The United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations Centre (UKMTO) reported 31 attacks in and around the Strait of Hormuz in October, and about 19 in November, as of Nov. 18.
Smoke billows from the Mayuree Naree, a Thailand-flagged bulk carrier, after it was hit by a projectile in the Strait of Hormuz, north of Oman, on March 11, 2026.
Previously, a total of 53 incidents had been reported to the UKMTO between March and September of this year, averaging 10 to 15 incidents total across both Strait of Hormuz and surrounding gulfs in previous months.
The International Maritime Organization (IMO), a United Nations agency, has slightly more conservative numbers, with 34 attacks confirmed in and around the Strait of Hormuz in October and November so far.
This too, is still a marked increase from previous numbers the IMO had collected, which number roughly 50 in and around the Strait of Hormuz between March and September. The IMO has tallied 138 attacks on vessels in total across the Middle East since the war began.
The positions of attacked tankers reported to the UKMTO indicate that most attacked vessels were in the very southern portion of the Strait of Hormuz, staying close to the Omani coastline, according to the maritime group's data.
Smoke rises at sea off the coast of Oman, Nov. 18, 2026, in this screengrab obtained from a social media video. A tanker was struck by an unknown projectile in its engine room while sailing outbound through the Strait of Hormuz, the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) said on Thursday.
"Iran's objective remains to keep the Omani route, which is described as a U.S.-facilitated route, a very high-risk passage and to keep the energy recovery inconsistent," Noam Raydan, senior fellow at the Washington Institute for Near East Policy, told ABC News.
Map identifying locations where vessels were attacked in the Strait of Hormuz in October and November of 2026, according to UKMTO data.
"Washington and its regional partners have found ways to keep oil flowing through the Strait of Hormuz," Hamidreza Azizi, senior Iran analyst at the International Crisis Group (ICG) think tank, told ABC News. "Tehran now seems determined to make these arrangements more costly and less reliable."
The workaround developed by the U.S. involves "ship-to-ship" (STS) transfers in which smaller tankers cross the strait with tracking systems switched off, and transfer cargos to larger tankers once safely on the other side, Sina Toossi, senior fellow with the Center for International Policy, told ABC News.
Iran is now responding in "a cycle of adaptation and counter-adaptation," he said.
"Tehran has escalated its attacks to make the STS system more dangerous, costly, and ultimately unviable. Iran's broader objective is to demonstrate that normal oil exports cannot continue while the US maintains its blockade of Iran, and to generate enough economic pressure to force Washington to negotiate an end to the conflict," Toossi said.
The U.S. has maintained a naval blockade, stopping Iranian and Iran-linked ships from going in and out of the Gulf of Oman, starting April 13, with a brief pause from June 18 to July 13.
Commercial vessels and oil tankers sit anchored in the waters off Bandar Abbas in southern Iran's Hormozgan Province on Sept. 9, 2026.
Strikes have not been limited to ships. On Nov. 8, Iran attacked the Omani island of Didamar in the strait itself, according to satellite images and video verified by ABC News.
The island hosts radar and satellite communications technology. Iranian state media said Iran had struck what it described as   "enemy navigation aid systems." Oman, a U.S. partner, did not comment on the attack.
Satellite image of Oman's Didamar island in the Strait of Hormuz following claimed Iranian attacks on infrastructure on the island.
Strikes have also not been isolated to ships actively crossing the strait. ABC News has verified at least one incident in which a ship was attacked by a drone appearing to belong to Iran, despite not making any attempt to cross the strait.
Bed bugs discovered in office at FEMA headquarters in DC
Famed Marine Corps veteran under federal investigation over undisclosed allegations
In early October, the Panama-flagged supertanker Gem No. 2 had been idle off the coast of the United Arab Emirates in the Persian Gulf, outside the Strait of Hormuz, for nearly five months.
It was fully loaded with a cargo of two million barrels of Saudi crude oil, per maritime intelligence company Kpler, and was one of the hundreds of ships the International Maritime Organization estimates is stuck in the Persian Gulf since the U.S. and Israel attacked Iran.
Two crew members who were on board Gem No. 2 say the ship never attempted to cross the Strait of Hormuz, and that it was attacked by one drone on Oct. 9 and then at least three others on Oct. 10, the latter attack sparking a massive fire and forcing the ship's evacuation, according to videos filmed by the crew obtained and verified by ABC News.
Oil Tanker Gem No2 on fire after being hit by drones while sitting idle off the coast of the United Arab Emirates in October 2026.
Hours after the vessel was struck for a second time and evacuated, the Iranian Revolutionary Guards Corps (IRGC) said in an online post that the vessel had struck a naval mine while attempting to cross the Strait of Hormuz through an "unauthorized" route.
Satellite images taken in the days after it was abandoned confirm Gem No. 2's position off the coast of the UAE, well outside the Strait of Hormuz.
Satellite image of oil tanker Gem No2 off the coast of the UAE on October 24, two weeks after being attacked.
ABC News showed images taken by the crew of the wreckage of the drone that struck the ship on Oct. 9 to Fabian Hinz, a researcher who studies drone warfare. Hinz said the wreckage in the images belongs to a jet-powered Hadid-110, built by Iran.   Iran continues to say the ship hit a mine.
Azizi, the ICG's Iran analyst, suggested that "large oil tankers seem to be receiving particular attention, whether they are moving through the strait or operating elsewhere in the Persian Gulf."
"One possible explanation is that Tehran wants to discourage the use of supertankers and prevent the development of alternative shipping arrangements that could make the blockade less effective," he said.
Pieces of a drone that hit oil tanker Gem No2 on October 9th, identified as an Iranian Hadid-110 drone by an expert to ABC News.
It's not clear why Gem No. 2 was allegedly targeted, but the vessel would have been an easy target, according to Samir Madani, co-founder of TankerTrackers.c o m . Madani told ABC News he noticed Gem No. 2 before the attack because the tanker's location transmission services were turned on, revealing its location publicly.
Both Azizi and Toossi describe Iran's actions in the Strait of Hormuz as having "strategic logic."
"Ultimately, the objective goes beyond disrupting oil exports. Iran is trying to demonstrate that the United States cannot guarantee maritime security in the Persian Gulf despite its overwhelming naval superiority," Azizi told ABC News.
Toossi added that this strategy will have consequences far beyond the strait.
"The danger is that this escalating contest will produce a much wider disruption of regional shipping and energy infrastructure, with even greater consequences for the global economy," he said.

Share Iran says it downed US drones over Hormuz as bid to end war remains stalled on social media
A US Air Force MQ-9 Reaper unmanned aerial vehicle used for long-endurance reconnaissance and strike missions [File: Ricardo Arduengo/Reuters]
Iranian forces say they have shot down two US drones over the Strait of Hormuz, as the United States steps up its economic pressure campaign against Iran.
The Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) said on Saturday a new air defence system had intercepted and shot down an MQ-9 drone, according to Iranian state broadcaster IRIB. It said the incident marked the 58th such drone brought down by Iranian forces since the start of the war nearly nine months ago.

list 2 of 3 Trump claims Iran is developing bioweapons: Is there any evidence?
list 3 of 3 US maritime agency warned Iran blockade was adding to rising Gulf premiums
Later on Saturday, the IRGC also claimed bringing down an MQ-1 drone over Qeshm Island in the Strait of Hormuz, the 19th such downing.
The incidents come days after the US and Iran engaged in direct, tit-for-tat strikes , against a backdrop of increasing Iranian attacks on vessels transiting the Strait of Hormuz, the vital waterway through which one-fifth of the world’s oil and gas passed in peacetime.
Launched by the US and Israel on February 28, the war has killed thousands of people and severely disrupted shipping, pushing global energy prices higher and spreading to countries across the region.
The US and Iran signed a memorandum of understanding in June, but it was never fully implemented because of disagreements over freedom and security of navigation in the Strait of Hormuz, with attacks resuming periodically since July. In August, The Washington Post reported that the US had lost 45 MQ-9 drones, or about 25 percent of its fleet at a cost of more than $1.3bn, during combat operations in Iran.
As an agreement to end the war remains elusive, Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi on Friday outlined his country’s positions on negotiations with the US, citing a seven-day proposal delivered to the US in September.
In an interview with state media, Araghchi said the seven conditions Iran has put forward “must be implemented for the Strait of Hormuz to reopen”. The conditions include ending the war and lifting sanctions and the naval blockade on Iran’s southern ports.
Araghchi said Iran was prepared to negotiate how the conditions should be implemented, saying its timetable was “flexible”. The negotiations would be “conditional on the American side taking necessary confidence-building measures”, he added.
The top diplomat also ruled out Iran transferring its stockpile of 60 percent enriched uranium abroad, but said a “fair solution” could be reached and a number of proposals by mediators were “worth examining”.
Araghchi said that the current “no war, no peace” state of the conflict was undesirable, but that Iran could not accept an agreement that would “hand victory to the other side”.
At a Friday news conference at the White House, US President Donald Trump told reporters that Tehran “want to make a deal” but not one that is acceptable to him.
“We want to make a real deal, not a fake deal that they’ve been doing for 51 years,” alleged Trump, who had said last week that a deal with Iran on ending the war was unnecessary.
At the same news conference, US Vice President JD Vance, who had previously blamed the war for Republicans losing both chambers of Congress earlier this month, declined to say whether he would have authorised strikes on Iran to prevent the country from developing a nuclear weapon.
Vance said the decision to attack Iran in February was Trump’s call, “and my job is to support the president of the United States.”
⁠Separately on Friday, the US Treasury ⁠⁠said it had imposed sanctions on four Iranians it said acted as “oil trustees”, collecting money from ⁠⁠illicit international oil sales for Iran to evade sanctions and the US naval blockade on its southern ports.
The Treasury said in a statement that ⁠⁠in many cases the trustees have kept oil revenues for personal gain. Among the individuals sanctioned are Mohammad Javad Bavand, a former IRGC intelligence officer, and Majid Taj, brother of ‌‌the Iranian Football Federation’s President Mehdi Taj, the Treasury said.
The new sanctions put ⁠⁠the individuals on the Treasury Office of Foreign Assets Control’s Specially Designated Nationals list, freezing any assets they may have under US jurisdiction and effectively prohibiting dollar ⁠⁠transactions with them or entities that they control.
The Treasury also said it imposed sanctions ⁠⁠on Mohammad Hossein Servati, the son of IRGC ⁠⁠Brigadier General Mohsen Servati, who has held positions in companies that brokered and received shipments of Iranian oil for delivery to independent Chinese “teapot” refineries.
Another sanctioned individual is ‌‌Mojtaba Arabnejad, the son of the sanctioned Mahan Air CEO Hamid Arabnejad. The Treasury said that Mojtaba Arabnejad has purchased aircraft ‌‌parts ‌‌for the sanctioned Mahan Air and overseen oil sales that have partly supported the airline.
Meanwhile, as Republicans grapple with the fallout from the sweeping midterm election losses, Democratic Representatives Yassamin Ansari and Ro Khanna called on Congress to use an upcoming government funding bill to end spending for offensive military operations against Iran.
Citing the mounting costs of the war, they issued a video statement urging fellow legislators to reject any funding package that keeps paying for the war, with a deadline looming next month to adopt a budget.
Failing to pass a spending bill by December 11 could trigger a government shutdown, a risk that has made some Democrats wary of drawing a red line on the war on Iran.
Rosa DeLauro and Patty Murray, the top Democrats responsible for appropriations, have said they would prefer to find ways to end the war without risking a government shutdown.

Oil Tankers Hit Near Strait of Hormuz as Farm Energy Risks Rise
Three oil tankers were hit near the Strait of Hormuz, raising concerns over global oil supplies, diesel prices and fertilizer costs for farmers worldwide.
Marcus Ellington is a U.S.-based journalist covering agricultural markets, global trade, and agricultural policy, with an international perspective on their impact across the global agri-food system.
At least three oil tankers were struck in or near the Strait of Hormuz on Saturday, November 21, 2026 , as military tensions involving Iran, the United States and Israel intensified around one of the world's most important energy shipping routes. The incidents raised fresh concerns about disruptions to global petroleum supplies and their potential impact on diesel prices, fertilizer production and agricultural transportation costs . For U.S. farmers, prolonged instability in the Persian Gulf could add pressure to operating expenses ahead of the 2027 planting season.
According to The Associated Press , the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations center reported that two tankers were struck by projectiles while leaving the Persian Gulf. No casualties were immediately reported. Iranian state media separately reported that another tanker struck a naval mine east of the strait and caught fire. Iran's navy also claimed it had conducted extensive military operations in the area overnight. The incidents highlight growing risks to commercial shipping , although the full extent of the damage and any resulting supply disruptions remained unclear.
New Bio-Based Pesticide Formulation Inhibits Nine Fungal Pathogens and Boosts Rice Root Growth
Diesel and Fertilizer Markets Face Growing Pressure
The Strait of Hormuz is a critical passage for international oil and liquefied natural gas shipments. Any prolonged interruption could increase shipping insurance premiums, transportation expenses and energy market volatility. Agriculture is particularly exposed to higher fuel costs , with diesel used extensively in tractors, combines, irrigation equipment and grain transportation. However, the attacks do not establish that U.S. farm fuel prices have already increased; their impact will depend on how energy markets respond.
Fertilizer markets could also face additional pressure , particularly nitrogen fertilizers such as ammonia and urea, whose production depends heavily on natural gas. Disruptions to Gulf energy exports or fertilizer shipping routes could influence international prices and availability. For American producers managing already significant input costs, changes in fertilizer quotations could affect purchasing decisions and crop budgets. The potential impact would vary by region, supplier contracts and the timing of fertilizer purchases.
The escalation comes as Iran continues demonstrating its military capabilities. AP reported that Iranian state television broadcast footage of a new dual-missile launcher at an underground facility, while Iranian officials maintained contact with Qatari mediators exploring diplomatic options. For agricultural markets, the immediate indicators to monitor are crude oil prices, diesel futures, fertilizer quotations and shipping costs , particularly if security conditions around the Strait of Hormuz deteriorate.

items.title: Zelensky says Crimean Bridge strikes 'fair response' as he meets UK's Streeting
items.summary: Ukraine's president says Kyiv acted after 109 separate Russian aerial attacks on bridges in Ukraine.
items.content:
Image caption, Wes Streeting told Volodymyr Zelensky he was in Kyiv to show that Europe was united in its support for Ukraine
By Sarah Rainsford ,Â  Southern and Eastern Europe correspondent in Kyiv Â  and Â  Jaroslav Lukiv
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky has justified Kyiv's repeated attacks on a critical bridge linking Russia to occupied Crimea, calling it a "fair response" to 109 separate Russian attacks on bridges in Ukraine.
In comments to the BBC in Kyiv, Zelensky said the intense attacks on Ukraine by Russia that have followed the strikes on the Crimean Bridge were only a "signal that Vladimir Putin does not want to stop. He wants a reason to escalate".
He rejected the claim by the Russian president that the bridge - which links Russia to the peninsula it illegally annexed from Ukraine - was "exclusively civilian" in use.
"There are facts, not just the words of Putin. We can see," he said.
The Ukrainian president pointed to images online of tanks and other Russian military hardware using the route from Russia into occupied Crimea as a supply line and for logistics.
The Ukrainian president added that Russia had carried out attacks with missiles and drones on bridges in Ukraine.
This week's combined missile-and-drone strikes by Ukrainian forces destroyed the central road section of the Crimean Bridge, collapsing part of it together with one of the two support arches into the sea and rendering the structure unusable for road traffic.
Russian attacks on Ukraine continued on Friday evening and overnight: a seven-year-old boy was killed in missile and drone strikes on Zelensky's hometown of Kryvyi Rih in the central Dnipropetrovsk region. Local officials say he had been in a playground at the time.
A 20-year-old female medic was also killed. A local official added that when rescuers rushed to the scene, the same site was targeted again with jet powered drones. Another 58 people were injured in the city.
Ukraine's state emergency service DSNS said 11 people were also injured in the north-eastern Kharkiv region, and one person in Rivne, in the north-west.
Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.
Figure caption, Footage shows Ukrainian missile approach Crimean Bridge
Zelensky was speaking ahead of a meeting in Kyiv with UK Defence Secretary Wes Streeting, who told the Ukrainian president he was here to show that Europe was united in its support.
"The more Putin tries to divide us, the more resolute we become," Streeting said.
He said that Russian missiles hitting Poland on Friday, during military exercises of the so-called Coalition of the Willing, was an "outrageous provocation".
The timing, Streeting said, seemed "more than a coincidence".
Asked by the BBC about Nato's response, he said the best way was to "do more for Ukraine" to defend itself against Putin who he called a "cold-blooded killer".
Streeting's description of Putin chimed with the comments made earlier by Zelensky, who described the Kremlin leader a "killer". This was done in response to US President Donald Trump referring this week to Putin as his "friend".
Streeting's visit to Kyiv came after European leaders meeting in Berlin on Thursday alongside US envoys said they were ready for negotiations with Moscow on ending the war in Ukraine.
"Europe has a clear and consistent and united negotiating position," UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham said, while German Chancellor Friedrich Merz stressed that Moscow's "maximalist demands are not realistic".
Donald Trump's son-in-law Jared Kushner, one of the two US envoys who were in Berlin, said the US president - who had also dialled into the meeting from Air Force One - wanted to make a deal with Moscow "with Europe by his side".
Russia's Vladimir Putin has so far rejected any European role in the US-led peace talks - but earlier this week he invited European representatives to Moscow as it wanted to clarify "what Europe will bring to these talks".
That meeting in the German capital came hours after Putin had held historic trilateral talks in Shenzhen, China, with Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping.
Zelensky said he had been "sceptical" ahead of the latest round of talks, when US envoys claimed that Russia was prepared to make compromises to end the war.
Speaking to the BBC, Streeting added: "Putin has absolutely no business playing the victim. He is the aggressor in this war. He provoked an illegal invasion of Ukraine. And all of us, right throughout the world, need to judge Putin not on his words, but on his actions."
In a separate development on Saturday, Finland said it "detected a drone strike on a Russian merchant vessel" in the eastern Gulf of Finland, "in an international maritime area".
The Finnish defence ministry said in a statement that the vessel was damaged, without giving any further details.
It added that "temporary restrictions on aviation and maritime areas in the eastern Gulf of Finland" were now reinstated for safety reasons.

items.content:
Pugh said the Strait of Hormuz has an "extraordinary natural world" beneath the surface
A British endurance swimmer has completed a three-day swim through the Strait of Hormuz to draw attention to what he says is the environmental cost of the conflict involving Iran.
Lewis Pugh, who is a UN Patron of the Oceans, swam about 15km (9.3 miles) through the strategic waterway, a key route for oil shipments from the Middle East.
Pugh, 56, who was born in Plymouth, Devon said "war causes immense human suffering" but nature is "another casualty that receives far too little attention".
He is calling for an end to the fighting, the reopening of the Strait of Hormuz and action to address environmental damage caused by the conflict.
The Strait of Hormuz carries a significant share of global oil shipments from the Middle East
The swimmer is believed to be the first person to attempt a long-distance swim in the Strait of Hormuz since the conflict began in March .
He swam from Musandam Island in the strait to the Cape of Hormuz, at the northern tip of Oman's Musandam Peninsula.
According to the Lewis Pugh Foundation, an oil tanker was struck by a projectile about 4km (2.5 miles) from where he was swimming on the first day.
On the second day, he saw flames rising above a headland separating him from the burning liquefied petroleum gas carrier Tara Gas and later passed close to the vessel while it was still on fire.
"My immediate thoughts were for the seafarers on board," Pugh said.
"The flames were enormous. These vessels carry highly flammable gases, and an attack on one can have catastrophic consequences - not just for crew members, but also on the surrounding marine environment."
Pugh has completed long-distance swims in every ocean of the world
Pugh said environmental damage caused by conflict often receives less attention than the human cost.
"War causes immense human suffering. Lives are lost, families are torn apart, and homes, hospitals and schools can be destroyed in minutes," he said.
"But there is another casualty that receives far too little attention: nature itself. And the damage can last long after the fighting has stopped."
The Strait of Hormuz is one of the world's most important shipping routes and is also home to wildlife including dugongs, sea turtles and whale sharks.
Pugh said oil spills and other contamination could have long-term consequences for marine ecosystems including coral reefs, seagrass meadows and mangrove forests.

The imposing architecture of a significant institution reflects the gravitas of central bank decisions, such as those anticipated from the Federal Reserve regarding future interest rate adjustments. © 24/7 Wall St.
Federal Reserve Governor Lisa Cook [ 1 ] told the Central Bank of Chile's annual conference in Santiago on November 20, 2026, that the Fed's single quarter-point hike in September is unlikely to change the path of inflation. If the Fed falls behind, she warned, "additional and larger rate increases may be required later to catch up."
The speech came on a bad day for stocks. The S&P 500 fell 3.70% to 6,910.39, and the Nasdaq Composite dropped 5.28%. The State Street SPDR S&P 500 ETF Trust ( NYSEARCA:SPY ) closed at $689.81, and delayed after-hours quotes later showed it at $697.30.
Treasury yields fell anyway. That leaves your index fund caught between a voting governor who says policy is too loose and a bond market pricing slower growth.
Cook framed the views as her own, with the larger hikes conditional, but she stopped short of calling for a half-point move in December.
Her case starts with inflation, which has run above the Fed's 2% [ 1 ] target for 67 months. She estimates October PCE prices rose 3.8% [ 1 ] over 12 months, and core PCE rose 3.2%, figures she built from recent data ahead of the official release.
She backed the September hike to a 3.75% to 4.00% [ 1 ] range, then was one of two October dissenters who wanted another increase. "In a different environment, the Committee could afford to be patient," she said, but she argued it lacks that luxury now.
Cook said policy is failing to slow the AI buildout, with companies announcing more than $2 trillion [ 1 ] in specific data center projects.
That expansion drives SPY. As of March 17, 2026, NVIDIA ( NASDAQ:NVDA | NVDA Price Prediction ) made up 7.58% of the fund, Apple ( NASDAQ:AAPL ) 6.66%, and Microsoft ( NASDAQ:MSFT ) 4.91%. The chipmakers get the headlines. But the power, cooling and networking suppliers feeding the data centers matter just as much, and we pulled seven of them into a free report .
Third-quarter GDP grew at a 3.4% [ 1 ] pace, and October payrolls rose 165,000. Rate hikes aimed at that strength hit high-valued growth stocks hardest.
The 2-year Treasury yield fell to 4.63% from 4.76% on Thursday, and the 10-year slipped to 4.92% from 5.04%. Yields falling during a hawkish speech suggest investors fear a slowdown more than they fear Cook.
Futures still priced about 92% odds of a quarter-point hike at the December 8-9 meeting. The VIX, a gauge of expected stock swings, closed at 28.44 [ 2 ] on November 19.
However, Cook's argument is still weak in some places.
"Behind the curve" means letting inflation outrun interest rates, so the Fed must later raise rates faster to regain control, and bigger hikes would pressure stock valuations and bond prices, lift yields on cash and raise mortgage and credit card costs.
But Cook is one voice and was outvoted in October. She also said equity prices are supporting consumer spending, and a deeper selloff would eat away that part of her own case.
Money needed within a few years carries the most exposure to this risk in SPY. A Fed debating bigger hikes while core inflation runs near 3.2% [ 1 ] is a poor background for a fund this concentrated in high-multiple technology.
Short-term Treasuries carry less valuation risk than stocks. The 2-year still yields 4.63%, a useful benchmark when researching how much rate risk SPY carries.
Watch the decision on December 9. If the Fed hikes by more than a quarter point or Cook gains company in dissent, her view is winning and SPY likely stays below $689.81. A single quarter-point hike with the 2-year holding under 4.76% would favor the bond market's slowdown view instead.

Military analyst Phillips O’Brien on Ukraine and Europe being left out of Trump's talks As President Trump met with Russian and Chinese counterparts, Ukraine and its European allies were left out of the talks.
NPR's Scott Simon talks with Phillips O'Brien of St. Andrew's University.
Military analyst Phillips O'Brien on Ukraine and Europe being left out of Trump's talks
Military analyst Phillips O’Brien on Ukraine and Europe being left out of Trump's talks
< iframe src="https://www.npr.org/player/embed/nx-s1-6047379/nx-s1-10014837" width="100%" height="290" frameborder="0" scrolling="no" title="NPR embedded audio player">
As President Trump met with Russian and Chinese counterparts, Ukraine and its European allies were left out of the talks.
NPR's Scott Simon talks with Phillips O'Brien of St. Andrew's University.
SCOTT SIMON, HOST: Two summits this week on two sides of the world. President Trump was in China with leader Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin, as European leaders gathered in Berlin with President Volodymyr Zelenskyy to show their support for Ukraine. We're joined now by Phillips O'Brien, professor of strategic studies at University of St. Andrews in Scotland. Professor, thanks for being back with us. PHILLIPS O'BRIEN: I'm (ph) glad to be here. SIMON: What do you think we learned from the two summits this week? O'BRIEN: Well, we've learned that the United States is now officially much closer to Russia than it is to Ukraine or its European partners and that the United States' goal is to now bully Ukraine into giving up territory and people to Russia so that Putin gets a very good deal. The other thing we've learned is that Ukraine's support now is going to come from Europe and Europe alone, that the United States - oh, and Canada. But that, you know, it is up to Europe now to work with Ukraine to fight Russia off. And that's the reality. It's been the reality for a while, but that's what we actually had confirmed this week. And that was a useful thing. SIMON: Is Europe up to it? O'BRIEN: It is, certainly. I mean, Europe is - you would say, if you stepped back, Europe's more than capable of helping Ukraine. It has the money. It has the technology. It has the people. It has the brainpower. It has the engineering. What it doesn't have is the ability to think strategically on its own. It's become, in some ways, infantilized by the United States over the past 80 years. The United States did so much of its strategic thinking. And Europeans are panicked, really, when faced with the reality of having to do it without the USA. They are slowly adjusting, but the real issue's not material. It's mental. SIMON: Ukraine carried out a major attack this week on Russia. They hit a bridge linking Russia with the occupied Crimea Peninsula. And Russia retaliated with deadly missile strikes in Volodymyr Zelenskyy's hometown yesterday. What does this tell us about the military capabilities of both countries? O'BRIEN: Well, what we know - Russia's plan is to try and break Ukrainian civilian will this winter by committing war crimes on a daily basis. And that's been the - what they've been doing for a while. So they're going to try to kill civilians. They're trying to freeze civilians. They're trying to cut power. They are going to try and make Ukraine as unlivable as possible. And they have been helped a great deal by the United States because the United States has deprived Ukraine of air defense. And right now, by the way, the United States and - through Starlink and Starshield is actually hampering Ukraine's ability to defend itself by shooting down drones. So the Russian strategy's quite straightforward in - when we see it in action. What the Ukrainians are trying to do is, in some ways, something far more ambitious and actually, by the way, legal. And that is they're trying to cut the flow of supplies to occupied western Ukraine. It's very hard for the Russians to get supplies into Crimea and then occupied parts of Kherson and Zaporizhzhia. And so what the Ukrainians seem to be trying to do is to isolate those regions and make it very difficult for the Russians to supply them. SIMON: The U.S. envoy Jared Kushner said he believes that Russia - his phrase was comfortable - is comfortable with... O'BRIEN: (Laughter). SIMON: ...NATO-like - well, you anticipate the question... O'BRIEN: (Laughter). SIMON: ...NATO-like security guarantees for Ukraine... O'BRIEN: Yeah. SIMON: ...As a way to end the war. Does this strike you as a plausible proposal for negotiations? O'BRIEN: Well, there's two things to say. NATO-like is nothing. Yeah, there's either NATO or not NATO. And, you know, NATO-like can be whatever they want it to be. But the key thing is Kushner's desperate to get a deal because they understand what's coming down the pike with the new Congress. And by the way, this was - they're saying it, oddly, to the Ukrainians and Europeans, who are then reporting it to the press, that what's going on is they - that, you know, Kushner and Witkoff and the Americans are saying, we need a deal by January 3 because we're going to have less power when the Democrats take over Congress. But this is simply posing. It's arguments, you know, that Putin is not going to accept anything like a real security guarantee for Ukraine. But it's the Trump administration's desperation to get something for Putin before the Democrats take over Congress. SIMON: It's been almost five years since Russia launched the full-scale invasion of Ukraine. It's a long time for Ukraine to hold out, isn't it? What's your sense of where the war might be heading? O'BRIEN: Well, it certainly is a long time, and they've done a remarkable job. And from the Ukrainian perspective, when you talk to them, their view is, we have no option. I mean, if we're - if we so - don't hold out, we'll be dead. I mean, it's quite clear that the Russians don't care about their lives, don't care about their cultures or societies. So resisting isn't really an option to them. They have to resist, or they will be wiped out. The thing that is very frustrating, and I got this from when I was last in Ukraine and talking to them, is they feel, in many ways, the war is heading in their favor. They're more adaptable. They're doing better on the front line. They were doing a very successful strike campaign against Russian oil refineries and logistics. But then the United States has, you know, come out and switched sides. And so the United States is providing a huge lifeline to Putin, which is really helping the Russians by leaving Ukrainian cities defenseless. And that's the reality of that - what they face. SIMON: Phillips O'Brien, professor at University of St. Andrews in Scotland. Thank you so much for being with us. O'BRIEN: Thank you.

Revolutionary Guards Navy says tanker was sailing ‘under US direction,’ warns of mines in restricted waters
ISTANBUL Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) Navy said Saturday that an oil tanker caught fire after striking a naval mine in a restricted area of the eastern Strait of Hormuz.
The naval command said in a statement that the tanker was sailing “under US direction” through the area when it struck the mine.
It warned ship captains and owners of the risk posed by mines in the area, saying it would hold them responsible for any damage resulting from the use of “unauthorized” routes.
Iran declared the Strait of Hormuz closed again on July 12, four days after the US resumed attacks on Iran. Tehran has threatened to target vessels that stray from its designated route or transit the strait without permission.

UN delegates at the Convention on Certain Conventional Weapons in Geneva. Photograph: Fabrice Coffrini/AFP/Getty
UN delegates at the Convention on Certain Conventional Weapons in Geneva. Photograph: Fabrice Coffrini/AFP/Getty
International UN talks on controlling use of autonomous weapons collapse
Week-long efforts fail to establish negotiating mandate on AI warfare after Russian ‘filibustering’
Week-long efforts to agree a negotiating mandate for a legally binding international treaty to control the use of autonomous weapons collapsed just before 5am after all-night talks failed to overcome Russian objections.
Despite an overwhelming majority of states at the UN’s Convention on Certain Conventional Weapons (CCW) in Geneva wanting to agree a negotiating mandate leading to a legally binding treaty, the need for consensus forced the conference to adopt a much weaker option.
The mandate asked countries “to elaborate by consensus”, an instrument that may not carry any legal obligations.
Although Russia led the objections using obstructive stalling tactics, other military powers invested in AI warfare, such as the US, were reluctant to commit to a legally binding protocol protecting civilians from robot drones and other autonomous weapons.
Delegates attend the UN Convention on Certain Conventional Weapons in Geneva. Photograph: Fabrice Coffrini/AFP/Getty Some argued that international humanitarian law was sufficient. More than 100 states had been pushing for a new law, saying the weapons raised entirely new challenges. European and Nato states, including Ukraine, China and Iran, expressed support or willingness for a new protocol.
The US said the need for human control over autonomous weapons had been discussed at the Apec summit in meetings between president Xi Jinping and Donald Trump this week, but the US was reluctant to agree a binding treaty.
South Korea, Japan, Turkey, the UK, France and Germany were among the defence tech powers exploring AI-enabled weapons who also expressed resistance to being bound by a new law, instead advocating for a nonbinding agreement.
The CCW is a UN forum that operates via consensus, meaning all 128 parties to the convention have to agree unanimously to pass a statement. The high threshold has resulted in the CCW failing to pass any new laws regulating weapons in the past 30 years and states seeking pathways elsewhere to pass treaties, such as the 2008 ban on cluster munitions.
The Future of Life Institute’s chair, Max Tegmark, said world leaders had failed to meet the moment this week. “Slaughterbots are already here,” he said. “Yet states have agreed it is sufficient to just talk about this for the 14th year.”
A campaign billboard is driven past the Houses of Parliament in London calling for control of AI weapons. Photograph: Andy Rain/EPA Diplomats inside the negotiations said Russia had been deliberately filibustering and not working in good faith, as opposed to the US delegates, who had been seeking a path to reach a consensus statement.
The exclusion of several nonmember countries from negotiations also prompted a rare protest in the chamber on the final day of the conference, with the Egyptian delegation shouting at the conference chair.
Israel and the US have also used AI-enabled targeting systems to conduct tens of thousands of strikes in Gaza and Iran, which have resulted in mass casualties. The Pentagon struck more than 1,000 targets in Iran on the first day of the war, and according to investigative media reports, the US military is aiming to carry out 1,000 AI-assisted targeting decisions per hour.
Critics said this outcome was a missed opportunity, noting that states had been discussing the issue of autonomous weapons, their dangers, and the need for international rules on how to restrict and regulate them for 13 years and large substantive parts of a treaty had already been settled upon.
One European diplomat said: “There was no political will to really regulate these weapons. No will commensurate to the urgency and need.”
A Human Rights Watch’s senior arms adviser, Bonnie Docherty, who had been directly involved in previously successful treaties banning cluster munitions and nuclear weapons, said autonomous weapons needed binding law. She noted that treaties could be negotiated within 15 months and dismissed the US’s proposal of five years to sort out a mandate.
A bloc of seven countries – Austria, Belgium, Brazil, Ireland, Mexico, New Zealand and Panama – had led the push for a binding treaty to be negotiated within one year.
On Wednesday Brazil’s delegate told the floor: “These are not weapons of the future being discussed here, these are already in use and being further developed. We are late in developing these norms and rules to regulate these lethal autonomous weapons systems.”

Home Iran News Now Iran Opposition & Resistance European Leaders Back ‘Third Option’ for Iran, Reject Appeasement, War and Return...
Iran Opposition & Resistance Latest News & Activities of Iran Protest Leader Maryam Rajavi
European Leaders Back ‘Third Option’ for Iran, Reject Appeasement, War and Return to Shah
NCRI President-elect Mrs. Maryam Rajavi addresses an international conference on November 21, 2026
Former European leaders, ministers and senior parliamentarians from several countries joined an international conference on Saturday, November 21, 2026, calling for a new policy toward Iran based on democratic change by the Iranian people rather than continued accommodation with Tehran or foreign military intervention. The conference, titled “The Third Option: Overthrow by the Iranian People and Resistance,” focused on the role of the organized Iranian Resistance and its Resistance Units inside the country, the surge in executions and repression, and what speakers described as the failure of Western policies toward Tehran. Participants also strongly rejected efforts to present Reza Pahlavi, son of the ousted Shah, as an alternative to the current regime, arguing that Iranians should not be forced to choose between religious and monarchical dictatorship.
Mrs. Maryam Rajavi, President-elect of the National Council of Resistance of Iran (NCRI), delivered the keynote address , arguing that the fundamental threat to the clerical authorities came not from external confrontation but from an increasingly restive society and an organized movement capable of turning popular revolt into political change.
Mrs. Rajavi said the military and political tensions surrounding Iran had obscured what she described as the central conflict determining the country’s future: the confrontation between the population and the ruling system.
“The central source of the regime’s existential crisis is the resistance of the Iranian people and society’s readiness for uprising and the regime’s overthrow,” she said. She pointed to the continuing operations of Resistance Units and rebellious youth, arguing that Tehran’s execution of PMOI members and protesters and the intensification of repression were attempts to prevent another uprising.
Marking the seventh anniversary of the November 2019 uprising, the NCRI President-elect said the protests had demonstrated both the scale of popular opposition and what an eventual confrontation over the regime’s survival could look like. She praised the protesters and Resistance Units involved in that uprising and said the authorities remained unable to resolve the threat posed by another nationwide revolt.
The Third Option Conference: Overthrow by the Iranian people and Resistance
We call on Europe to adopt a firm policy toward this regime.
And the clearest expression of such resolve is to stand with the Iranian people and their Resistance in their struggle to overthrow the… pic.twitter.com/ntf65KrMX7
— Maryam Rajavi (@Maryam_Rajavi) November 21, 2026
Mrs. Rajavi framed the political alternative in explicit terms.
“We have said that the solution to the Iranian crisis lies neither in appeasement nor in foreign war,” she said. “The developments of the past year have put this proposition to the test.”
She said change had to come through “a force rooted in Iranian society and independent of foreign powers,” one that had established its credentials in the struggle against both the Shah’s dictatorship and clerical rule.
“This is the Third Option: overthrow by the Iranian people and their organized Resistance, spearheaded by the Resistance Units and the Liberation Army.”
Mrs. Rajavi described the Resistance Units and Iran's rebellious youth as the force underlying Tehran’s continuing fear of another uprising. She linked executions of imprisoned PMOI members, repression of protesters, surveillance and the regime’s foreign conflicts to what she called its fear of this domestic opposition.
She also sharply criticized Western efforts to elevate remnants of the former monarchy, saying such initiatives ultimately assisted Tehran by allowing it to portray the political alternatives as either continuation of clerical rule or restoration of the Shah.
Watch Live: European politician meet to discuss concern about Iran's threat to continent https://t.co/O4S5YjKSeN
— John Solomon (@jsolomonReports) November 21, 2026
“The key to change lies in the hands of the Iranian people and the Iranian Resistance,” Mrs. Rajavi said, describing a movement that had “endured through fire and blood for 45 years” under the slogan “Neither Shah nor Mullahs.” She said the NCRI sought a secular democratic republic based on gender equality, autonomy for oppressed nationalities, abolition of the death penalty and a non-nuclear foreign policy.
Mrs. Rajavi called on European governments to condition relations with Tehran on an end to executions and the killing of protesters, close Iranian embassies she accused of serving as centers for espionage and terrorism, and formally recognize the Iranian people’s struggle against the regime and the struggle of rebellious youth against the IRGC.
Former European Council President and Belgian Prime Minister Charles Michel said Europe and the United States had to fundamentally rethink their approach to Iran.
“We tried appeasement, we got more oppression. We tried concessions and negotiations, we got blackmail and hostage-taking,” Michel said. “We witnessed military confrontation, and we got more destruction and suffering, and the regime is still there.”
He drew three conclusions: the clerical authorities would not reform; foreign military intervention could not deliver democracy; and democratic change led by Iranians themselves should become “the cornerstone of European policy.”
Michel said the claim that Iran lacked an organized alternative was itself part of Tehran’s propaganda.
“There is indeed an alternative. It did not appear yesterday,” he said. “For more than four decades, Iranian men and women have risked everything to keep the flame of freedom alive. The MEK and its Resistance Units on the ground are at the forefront of this struggle.”
Former EU Council President @CharlesMichel urges 3 lessons for the EU on Iran:
2⃣ Foreign war can't deliver democracy—We don't have to choose between appeasement vs. war.
3⃣ The alternative: democratic change led by Iran's people.
CC: @kajakallas https://t.co/PZUYnu4yIs pic.twitter.com/dUy4zLviUn
— M. Hanif Jazayeri (@HanifJazayeri) November 21, 2026
Addressing Resistance members inside Iran and at Ashraf 3, Michel added: “You are not spectators of history; you are making history.”
He described the NCRI as a political alternative with a program, support inside Iran and an international network, and said Mrs. Rajavi’s Ten-Point Plan supplied a democratic framework for the transition.
Michel also rejected Pahlavi as an alternative. He criticized the former Shah’s son for praising his father’s legacy and for advocating foreign military intervention, and said hereditary status could not confer democratic legitimacy.
“The people of Iran do not need a would-be king; they need democracy,” Michel said. “We cannot oppose one dictatorship while opening the door to another one. The future of Iran belongs neither to the Shah nor to the mullahs; it belongs to the Iranian people.”
Former Speaker of the UK House of Commons John Bercow similarly said Tehran could neither be transformed through accommodation nor removed through war.
“What we know about the regime is that it cannot be improved by appeasement or removed by war,” he said.
Bercow devoted a large portion of his remarks to Pahlavi, arguing that his continued defense of his family’s record, his lack of democratic mandate and the role he proposed for himself in a future political system disqualified him as a credible republican alternative.
Vanmorgen om 4 uur opgestaan om mijn Iraanse vrienden bij te staan en hen te steunen bij het bereiken van iets wat voor ieder mens vanzelfsprekend zou moeten zijn: in vrede leven in je eigen land, zonder bang te hoeven zijn voor de overheid.
Onder de aanwezigen waren John… pic.twitter.com/ieKwd3NvXe
— Dorien Rookmaker (@RookmakerDorien) November 21, 2026
He described Pahlavi as “a prince without a people” and “a relic of royal rule,” and argued that his promotion diverted international attention from the organized opposition inside Iran.
Bercow contrasted that with what he described as nearly five decades of sacrifice by the NCRI and PMOI.
“Courage, conviction, commitment,” and compassion, he said, were characteristics he associated with Mrs. Rajavi and the organized Resistance. Those qualities, he added, had been “forged in the furnace over almost five decades of service, of sacrifice, and of struggle.”
Bercow pointed to the Ten-Point Plan’s commitments to freedom of speech, association and the press, separation of religion and state, minority rights, gender equality, universal suffrage, abolition of capital punishment and a non-nuclear republic.
He also emphasized what he saw as a fundamental difference between Pahlavi’s political project and the Resistance: the latter, he said, was built around a cause rather than personal advancement.
“These people have made a lifelong commitment to serve a cause,” Bercow said.
“The future of Iran does not belong to a prince because of his birth. It does not belong to a cleric because of his title. And it does not belong to a politician because of his ambition. It belongs to the people of Iran themselves.”
Former European Commission Vice President and former EU Commissioner Mairead McGuinness placed the Iranian crisis within a broader erosion of democratic institutions worldwide and warned that both war and internal repression were compounding the suffering of Iranians.
Citing the UN Special Rapporteur on Iran, she noted that Iranians had been caught between “external aggression and internal repression” and said war had not reduced repression but had intensified it.
— Dorien Rookmaker (@RookmakerDorien) November 21, 2026
McGuinness stressed that a successful democratic transition required more than the removal of a dictatorship. It demanded durable institutions capable of preventing another concentration of power: independent courts, parliamentary oversight, electoral integrity, free media, minority protections and genuine political competition.
“In a true democracy, people have the right to choose a government, criticize it, oppose it, and replace it peacefully at the next election,” she said.
She said the desire for democracy among Iranians was evident, particularly among young people, but warned that the transition would require “courage and determination” and broad agreement on the institutions and political rules of a future Iran.
Former German Defense Minister Franz Josef Jung , now president of the association representing former members of the Bundestag and European Parliament, said the best way out of Iran’s crisis was replacement of the existing system with democratic government.
Jung argued that the regime’s increasing repression and fear of opposition were signs of weakness, while its regional activities and nuclear program also threatened European security.
He said nationwide protests had demonstrated Iranians’ rejection of both “the ruling mullahs’ dictatorship” and “a return to the monarchic dictatorship of the Shah’s era.”
“The ‘Reza Pahlavi’ alternative… is simply not credible,” Jung said, arguing that Pahlavi had neither repudiated his father’s abuses nor clearly separated himself from the Revolutionary Guards.
The Third Option Conference: Overthrow by the Iranian people and resistance
We gather here at a time when our country, Iran, remains at the epicenter of a regional and international upheaval.
Change in Iran comes through a force proven in the struggle against both the Shah’s… pic.twitter.com/pc8ut11svj
— Maryam Rajavi (@Maryam_Rajavi) November 21, 2026
Jung said Mrs. Rajavi’s Ten-Point Plan , including free elections, political freedoms, separation of religion and state, gender equality, judicial independence, abolition of torture and the death penalty and a non-nuclear Iran, should receive explicit European Union support.
Former Polish Foreign Minister Anna Fotyga , who previously chaired the European Parliament’s Subcommittee on Security and Defense, drew on Poland’s experience with the Solidarity movement and resistance to Soviet rule.
Fotyga said decades of repression under both the Shah and clerical rule demonstrated the cost paid by Iranians seeking freedom. She emphasized, however, that opposition to Tehran required more than denunciations from abroad.
“We have not only to condemn, and not only diplomatically to support, but we have to know that Iran has a well-organized opposition—really well organized, very prudent, caring for people, their security in particular, and their well-being,” she said.
Fotyga praised what she described as the Resistance’s long-developed leadership, organization and caution in confronting a heavily armed dictatorship, saying those qualities had made it easier for her to support the movement during her years in the European Parliament.
Lithuanian parliamentarian Emanuelis Zingeris , deputy head of his country’s delegation to the Parliamentary Assembly of the Council of Europe, compared Iran’s political prisoners with dissidents who resisted Soviet rule in Central and Eastern Europe.
He highlighted the case of political prisoner Mohammad Javad Vafaei Sani , recipient of a Magnitsky Human Rights Award and repeatedly sentenced to death. Quoting from a message attributed to Vafaei Sani, Zingeris said: “I remain steadfast in my pledge, and I will not bow before oppression until the people of Iran will be free.”
Zingeris urged Europe to treat human rights and freedom as strategic priorities rather than subordinating them to economic concerns, and pledged continued support for the Iranian democratic movement. He also called for implementation of measures targeting the IRGC and said democratic countries should unite around “extremely visible support for the freedom of the Iranian people.”
German Bundestag member and Judiciary Committee chair Carsten Müller said Iran’s future could not be secured by replacing one form of dictatorship with another.
“Iran and the Iranian people are not helped if they are shifted from one terribly bloodthirsty dictatorship into another, monarchist dictatorship,” Müller said. “The Iranian people want to be free, and we want to help them in that and stand by their side.”
He also rejected reliance on foreign military action.
“We cannot rely on help coming from the outside, or on a military intervention bringing freedom to the Iranian people,” Müller said. “The Iranian people want to win freedom themselves, they can win it themselves.”
Fellow Bundestag member Detlef Seif focused on repression both inside Iran and beyond its borders. He cited Germany’s measures against transnational repression and called for sustained action against IRGC structures, including investigation of financial networks and operations in Europe.
Seif said German and EU policy toward Iran had been “far too restrained” and argued that neither diplomacy nor sanctions alone were sufficient.
At the same time, he explicitly rejected foreign-imposed regime change.
“We do not want an active contribution when it comes to a war that we carry into Iran, or regime change from the outside,” Seif said. “But what we can do and what we should do is support this democratic opposition, this freedom movement,” through measures consistent with international law.
The Third Option Conference: Overthrow by the Iranian people and Resistance

— Maryam Rajavi (@Maryam_Rajavi) November 21, 2026
Italian MP Naike Gruppioni , a member of the Chamber of Deputies’ Foreign Affairs Committee, focused on executions, women and political prisoners. She said diplomatic convenience, economic interests and political calculations could not justify silence over repression.
Addressing Iranian women directly, Gruppioni said: “You are not victims to be pitied; you are protagonists in a battle for freedom.”
She called on Europe to go beyond statements of concern and demand an end to executions, the release of political prisoners, an end to persecution of women and accountability for those responsible for repression.
Gruppioni also rejected war as an answer and warned against replacing the current system with another authoritarian structure.
“Iran does not need a new dictatorship, nor an authority with a different face but the same claim to control citizens’ lives,” she said.
She reaffirmed her support for Mrs. Rajavi’s Ten-Point Plan and said a genuine democratic transformation could not occur without women being fully represented in political decision-making.
Italian MP Alfredo Antoniozzi , vice president of the Brothers of Italy parliamentary group and a former member of the European Parliament, said Iran’s crisis would be solved neither through military force nor through negotiations confined to governments.
“I do not believe that this issue will be resolved with bombs, nor merely through negotiations between governments, which remain on the surface,” Antoniozzi said. “We must go deeper.”
He argued that democratic societies had a responsibility to demonstrate to Iranians that broad international public opinion supported their struggle for freedom and political dignity.

“For more than four decades, the NCRI and the PMOI have built an organized, democratic alternative while championing women’s leadership,” former UK International Development Minister Baroness Verma , a member of the House of Lords said. She described the movement, as democratic Muslims, as an antithesis to religious fundamentalism and said Mrs. Rajavi’s Ten-Point Plan offered a “modern, inclusive, and progressive” framework based on a pluralistic democratic republic, gender equality, abolition of the death penalty and rejection of nuclear weapons.
Former President of the European Council, Prime Minister of Belgium, Charles Michel
addresses an international conference on November 21, 2026
Baroness Verma also called for stronger accountability measures against Iranian officials. She urged governments to make greater use of universal jurisdiction and said the recent proscription of the IRGC had to be followed by enforcement against its assets, financial networks and individuals benefiting from wealth accumulated outside Iran.
“If we are going to be serious,” she said, governments needed to “crack down on those people and their properties, their assets, and all they have accumulated outside of Iran.”
Fellow House of Lords member Lord Steve McCabe focused on executions, political prisoners and the need for governments to engage directly with the organized opposition. Referring to death-row political prisoner and Magnitsky Human Rights Award recipient Mohammad Javad Vafaei Sani, Lord McCabe said his case reflected both the authorities’ reliance on executions and the persistence of resistance inside the country.
He also rejected preferential treatment for Reza Pahlavi by Western governments. While saying Pahlavi was entitled to put his case before Iranians, Lord McCabe argued that Iran’s future could not be determined by advocates of hereditary monarchy or preservation of religious tyranny.
“It must be the result of free and fair elections,” he said.
Lord McCabe said his experience of more than 20 years with the PMOI and NCRI had led him to view the movement as a credible democratic alternative.
“This movement offers a credible, democratic alternative to the ruling theocracy and deserves international recognition and political support,” he said, urging the British government and other European states to engage directly with the NCRI.
He stressed that the Resistance was not asking foreign governments to wage war on its behalf. “The Resistance isn't asking Western governments to fight its battle,” Lord McCabe said. “It's seeking political support for the Iranian people's legitimate struggle for freedom, justice, and democracy.”
Former Norwegian Climate and Environment Minister Ola Elvestuen said international attention should focus less on the external dimensions of the Iranian crisis and more on what he described as the regime’s struggle against its own population.
“They fear the enemy within: a society demanding change and a resistance determined to achieve it,” Elvestuen said. He argued that the appropriate response was “not appeasement, but supporting the opposition and those who fight for a free and democratic Iran.”
Former UK House of Commons Speaker John Bercow addresses an international conference on November 21, 2026
Elvestuen also linked political repression with Iran’s environmental crisis, citing water shortages, land subsidence, drying lakes and wetlands, air pollution and deforestation as further consequences of systemic mismanagement.
He concluded by rejecting the choice between clerical rule and monarchical restoration.
“The choice is not between the mullahs and another Shah,” Elvestuen said. “The democratic alternative is the organized resistance.” He said Europe should maintain pressure over executions, accountability and human rights while supporting the Iranian people and their Resistance.
Former German ambassador Dr. Hans-Ulrich Seidt , who previously served as Germany’s ambassador to Afghanistan and Korea and as Inspector General of the German Foreign Office, presented a strategic assessment of the internal opposition based on a study he co-authored with Bundestag Judiciary Committee chairman Carsten Müller.
Amb. Seidt said three decades of European diplomacy aimed at managing and moderating Tehran had failed, while military force had also failed to produce democratic change.
“Neither in Iraq nor [in Afghanistan] could democracy be achieved from outside through the use of military force,” he said. “Is there another, a third option? Yes.”
That third option, Amb. Seidt said, was the organized opposition inside Iran.
He argued that spontaneous protest, however significant, was not sufficient to overthrow an entrenched dictatorship. An effective opposition, he said, required organization, structures inside the country, accumulated experience, a coherent political program and leadership.
“What impresses me about the Mojahedin and the National Council of Resistance is that you have this experience, across generations,” Amb. Seidt said.
He pointed to Resistance members who had fought the Shah in the 1970s, subsequent generations who continued the opposition in later decades, and young activists now building on that experience.
Seidt also cited Mrs. Rajavi’s Ten-Point Plan as evidence of a developed political program and argued that the NCRI possessed both organizational continuity and leadership.
He urged European governments to overcome longstanding reluctance to engage with the PMOI and NCRI.
European Union Special Envoy for the Promotion of Freedom of Religion or Belief Mairead McGuinness addresses an international conference on November 21, 2026
“European foreign policy must be ready to conduct dialogue with the democratic opposition,” Seidt said.
He argued that Tehran’s own efforts to suppress the PMOI should be understood as evidence of its significance: “When the Iranian regime says that the Mojahedin are the most dangerous opposition, it is an indicator of how important and how relevant this opposition is.”
Amb. Seidt concluded that Iranians alone must decide their country’s future, while Europe’s role was to support those who had worked and sacrificed “for generations for a free and democratic Iran.”
Former Norwegian parliamentarian Lars Rise similarly argued that opposition to the existing regime was not enough by itself. The decisive question, he said, was which political force possessed “the principles, the organization, and the capacity to replace it.”
Rise criticized efforts to promote Pahlavi internationally and said Iran required “a democratic alternative rooted in the people's struggle, not a manufactured substitute promoted from abroad.”
He said that alternative had to combine rule of law, political freedom, social cohesion and democratic organization, adding that he saw those principles reflected in Rajavi’s Ten-Point Plan.
Rise, who said he had worked alongside the Iranian Resistance for nearly 30 years, emphasized the movement’s endurance as another measure of its credibility. He concluded that his support would continue for as long as necessary, saying that if required, he was “ready to fight for another 30 years.”
Former German Defense Minister Franz Josef Jung addresses an international conference on November 21, 2026
Former European Parliament Vice President Alejo Vidal-Quadras , now president of the International Committee in Search of Justice, said Europe had persisted for decades with a fundamentally flawed approach toward Tehran even as the regime became increasingly vulnerable.
“There is a profound paradox in Europe’s policy towards Iran,” Dr. Vidal-Quadras said. “While the Iranian regime is isolated, weakened, vulnerable, and despised by its people, European diplomacy continues to treat it as an indispensable partner.”
He argued that decades of engagement, concessions and accommodation had been interpreted in Tehran as weakness and had produced “warmongering, hostage-taking, and terrorism.”
Dr. Vidal-Quadras also referred to the November 2023 assassination attempt against him in Madrid, which he said was linked to his support for the PMOI, NCRI and Maryam Rajavi . He said the case demonstrated that Tehran’s repression extended beyond Iran’s borders.
“Supporting the NCRI and PMOI is not just a political position. It means taking a serious risk,” he said.
Turning to Iran’s domestic situation, Dr. Vidal-Quadras cited the growing number of executions and said European policymakers remained trapped by the assumption that the regime was permanent despite repeated uprisings.
“The Iranian people demand fundamental change, rejecting both the past dictatorship of the Shah and the current criminal rule of the mullahs,” he said.
He sharply rejected efforts to promote Reza Pahlavi, arguing that Western attempts to give him legitimacy damaged Iran’s democratic movement. “The Iranian people must never be forced to choose between two dictatorships,” Dr. Vidal-Quadras said, adding that genuine transition required pluralism, free elections, gender equality, separation of religion and state and abolition of the death penalty.
He called on Europe to end what he described as the illusion that concessions could moderate Tehran, make an end to executions and the release of political prisoners central conditions for relations, act against the IRGC and its transnational networks, and recognize the Iranian people’s right to resist dictatorship.
Member of UK House of Lords Baroness Verma addresses an international conference on November 21, 2026
“The future of Iran belongs to them alone, to the people alone,” Dr. Vidal-Quadras said. “And it is our duty to support them and their organized resistance in their struggle for freedom, justice, and democracy.”
Former European Parliament member Dorine Rookmaker said the regime’s intensifying repression should be understood as evidence of its fear of domestic opposition.
Addressing political prisoners, Resistance Units and members of the movement at Ashraf 3, Rookmaker said: “The more we see the regime being oppressive and aggressive, the more we know they fear you. They fear you. It’s a point of weakness, a sign of weakness.”
She also highlighted what she described as the leading role of women in both nationwide uprisings and the organized Resistance.
Rookmaker contrasted that model with Pahlavi, saying he offered no credible political vision and relied on foreign powers rather than Iran’s own population.
“Beyond being the son of the deposed Shah, he offers no credible vision for Iran’s future,” she said. “His campaigning divides rather than unites.”
She cited the cases of political prisoners Zahra Tabari and Arghavan Fallahi , and quoted Fallahi as saying: “We, our generation, Generation Z, oppose dictatorship and dependency. We stand against both the Shah and the mullahs.”
Rookmaker described Mrs. Rajavi’s Ten-Point Plan as a clear democratic alternative based on freedom, human rights, gender equality and free elections, and urged governments to “engage seriously with the NCRI as a democratic alternative.”
Member of Parliament; Head, Seimas Delegation to the Parliamentary Assembly of the Council of Europe Emanuelis Zingeris addresses an international conference on November 21, 2026
A member of the Parliament of Estonia Juku-Kalle Raid said Estonia’s own history under Soviet occupation had taught its people the danger of Western calls for caution toward authoritarian systems.
Recalling how some in Western Europe once cautioned against “rocking the Soviet boat,” he said the same logic should not now be applied to Tehran.
“We wanted freedom,” he said. “It was like someone from the free world saying now: ‘Don’t rock the mullahs’ boat.’ Is that okay? No. It isn’t okay.”
Raid said information about Iran’s repression had to be carried back to “every parliament” and “every country,” and noted that a significant portion of Estonian MPs had publicly supported a free Iran.
He also mocked the idea of hereditary restoration and said Iranians should instead have free speech, free media, free elections and the right both to vote and to stand for office.
“Every Iranian citizen should have an opportunity for free speech, free media, free elections,” he said.
Fellow Estonian parliamentarian Ando Kiviberg , chair of the parliament’s Constitutional Committee, said the central issue in struggles against dictatorship was political will.
“There’s no such thing as an eternal, forever-lasting dictatorship regime in human history,” Kiviberg said. “For any regime, for any dictatorship, there is an end.”
He argued that Europe also needed the determination to support those fighting for freedom, warning against the temptation in prosperous democracies to avoid involvement in struggles elsewhere.
Kiviberg called for accountability for those responsible for executions and repression.
“Behind every execution, behind every crime committed in the name of the regime, are individuals,” he said, urging governments to make clear that those responsible would ultimately be brought to justice.
He concluded by pledging Estonian support for Iranians seeking freedom and said his country would continue pressing European politicians to provide whatever support was possible.
Italian Member of Parliament Naike Gruppioni addresses an international conference on November 21, 2026
Argentine lawmaker Damián Arabia said his country’s experience with terrorism attributed to Tehran gave Argentina a particular stake in confronting the Iranian regime.
He cited the 1992 bombing of the Israeli Embassy in Buenos Aires and the 1994 AMIA Jewish community center bombing, as well as the death of prosecutor Alberto Nisman shortly before he was due to testify before Congress about the AMIA investigation.
Arabia said Argentina would not be intimidated and noted that his government had designated the IRGC as a terrorist organization.
He also said a parliamentary majority in Argentina had supported the Iranian Resistance’s Ten-Point Plan and argued that the Iranian people had the right to determine their future free of both religious dictatorship and monarchy.
“We believe the Iranian people have the right to decide their own future,” Arabia said, describing that future as one “without religious dictatorship, without political executions, without any repression, and without any Shah.”
He called instead for a democratic, secular and pluralistic republic based on equal rights for women and men.
Geneva parliamentarian Patrick Lussi said Iran faced both a deep human-rights crisis and a crisis of political legitimacy, but argued that continued repression had been met by “an exceptional resistance.”
He criticized what he described as fruitless engagement with Tehran and said “the time for dialogue without conditions and without concrete results” should end.
“At the same time, we must support the other face of Iranian reality,” Lussi said, referring to “an organized resistance that fights for freedom, democracy, justice and human dignity.”
Lussi called on Switzerland to designate the IRGC as a terrorist organization, adopt a parliamentary resolution condemning executions, and deny entry to senior Iranian officials implicated in repression and human-rights violations.
He also endorsed Mrs. Rajavi’s Ten-Point Plan , citing its commitments to a democratic republic, separation of religion and state, gender equality, abolition of the death penalty, human rights and peaceful coexistence.

items.title: Two tankers hit in Strait of Hormuz as hawks press Trump to resume Iran strikes - New York Post
items.summary: Two tankers hit in Strait of Hormuz as hawks press Trump to resume Iran strikes  New York Post
items.content:
Two tankers were reportedly struck by projectiles near the Strait of Hormuz Saturday, raising fears of a new escalation in the crucial oil-shipping corridor as Israel and administration hawks press President Trump to renew major attacks on Iran.
One tanker attempting to leave the strait was struck in the stern, according to the UK Maritime Trade Operations agency, while a second reported a projectile hitting its engine room. No casualties were reported.
Since the US war with Iran began in late February, more than 120 commercial vessels have been attacked in and around the Strait, killing at least 24 seafarers, according to the International Maritime Organization.
Two tankers were hit in Strait of Hormuz Saturday, according to the UK's Maritime Trade Office. Here a liquefied petroleum gas tanker burns in the Strait of Hormuz on Tuesday, Nov. 17, 2026. Lewis Pugh Foundation via AP
October accounted for 28 attacks, the highest single-month toll of the conflict.
Trump is facing calls from inside and outside his administration to resume major attacks on Iran that have been on pause since the summer, despite repeated strikes and counter strikes in the region.
Israel's ambassador to the US, Michael Leiter, told The Post this week that his country "believes ousting the Tehran regime is now the only long- or even medium-term answer," adding that Israel "will not hesitate to go it alone" because the situation is "existential."
Leiter also faced backlash after telling Newsmax: “You get American soldiers back here to the United States, to their families, when Iran is defeated.”
Iran's Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi mocked the remarks on X. “We did not know that the Israeli Ambassador to Washington was the commander-in-chief of the U.S. Military,” he wrote.
Amid the backlash, Leiter sought to make clear that he was not suggesting Israel could dictate US military policy.
"Let's state the obvious: only the President of the United States decides when and where American troops are deployed," he wrote on X.
Hawks within the US administration are pushing to resume strikes as well, Britain’s Financial Times reported.
US Central Command has reportedly warned officials about the strain a prolonged military buildup is placing on American forces, even as congressional Democrats prepare to challenge funding for the campaign.
“Centcom is telling the administration that they’re running out of time, burning money and readiness,” a source told the paper. A US official disputed that characterization.
President Trump on Friday accused Iran of refusing to negotiate a deal acceptable to Washington.
"They want to make a deal, but they don't want to make a deal that's acceptable to me. We want to make a real deal, not a real deal that they've been doing for 51 years," he told reporters.
"They've been bull——g people for 51 years," he added.
Trump repeated his vow that "Iran will never have a nuclear weapon ever,” but his administration faces a potential congressional battle over the cost of the conflict as Democrats prepare to take control of both chambers.
Iran, meanwhile, appears to be preparing a challenge to the US naval blockade.
"They've been bull——g people for 51 years," President Trump told reporters at the White House. AFP via Getty Images
More than a dozen Iranian oil tankers have reportedly gathered near Kharg Island, the country's principal oil-export terminal, as Tehran weighs ways to move crude despite the blockade, Defense News reported.
Iran's state-affiliated Fars News Agency has floated the idea of a tanker convoy through the Gulf of Oman to get Iranian oil to market.
The US has launched repeated strikes on Iran's Qeshm Island this month , while Iran has continued to lob attacks at US allies, including targeting drone and missile strikes at Kuwait .

On the nuclear front, Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said Iran had not changed its official position on nuclear weapons despite international pressure and debate over its nuclear doctrine.
China and Russia oppose any change in Tehran's nuclear doctrine, Araghchi said, according to Iran Daily.
"What matters is that, up to this point, our doctrine has not changed, and our official positions remain the same as before," Araghchi said.
Iran is a signatory to the Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty, but its nuclear program has long drawn international scrutiny over undeclared activities, underground facilities and restrictions on UN inspections.
Washington has accused Tehran of seeking the capability to build nuclear weapons.
