items.content:
Iran prepares oil tanker convoy to break US naval blockade, threatens Gulf facilities - report
Iran is reportedly preparing a convoy of more than 14 oil tankers to challenge the US naval blockade, as media outlets close to the IRGC threaten attacks on Gulf energy infrastructure.
A Cargo boat navigates the sea on April 28, 2026 on Qeshm Island, Iran in the Strait of Hormuz. (Illustrative)
Iran is reportedly preparing to send a convoy of more than 14 oil tankers through the US naval blockade in the coming days, as Iranian media outlets affiliated with the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) threaten strikes on Gulf energy facilities if American forces intervene, according to satellite tracking data and Iranian media reports.
The tankers are reportedly assembling near Kharg Island , the departure point for approximately 85% to 90% of Iran's crude oil exports.
According to satellite imagery and vessel-tracking data, the tankers are crewed and flying Iranian flags, and Tehran reportedly plans to send the convoy toward the Gulf of Oman in the coming days.
The Persian-language service of Euronews described the information as "unofficial reports." No independent confirmation has emerged that the convoy has departed.
TankerTrackers, a company that monitors oil tankers using satellite imagery, said its data suggested Iran was preparing to resume oil exports.
US forces operating in the Strait of Hormuz, July 17, 2026. (credit: Screenshot/X/@PeteHegseth)
Samir Madani, a co-founder of the company, told Reuters on Thursday that a tanker was receiving Iranian crude oil from another vessel in the Gulf.
"If it leaves the blockade area, this will be the first successful seaborne export of Iranian crude oil since mid-July," he said.
Madani did not identify the tanker but said it was not subject to US Treasury Department sanctions.
According to Asharq Bloomberg , approximately 200,000 barrels of Iranian oil were transferred between the tankers Olim and Hao Fan near Kharg Island. Both vessels reportedly switched off their tracking systems during the transfer.
The report described it as the first ship-to-ship oil transfer identified since the blockade was reinstated.
Iranian media propose sending tanker convoy through US blockade
The reported preparations follow the publication of a column on Wednesday by the Fars News Agency, which is affiliated with the IRGC, outlining a proposal to break the US blockade.
"To break the naval blockade, Iran can move a group of tankers that will break through," the column stated.
Under the proposal, Tehran would warn that any US military attempt to attack or detain the tankers would trigger immediate Iranian strikes against regional energy infrastructure, particularly oil facilities in the United Arab Emirates.
Similar proposals appeared two days earlier in Hamshahri Online and the Young Journalists Club (YJC).
Iranian media outlets have begun referring to the proposal as the "Fereydun Plan," named after a scene from the Shahnameh, the Persian epic.
Iranian politicians have also called for a more assertive response to the blockade.
Iranian parliament member Mohammad Bayat said on Friday that Tehran needed to abandon its passive approach amid a situation of "neither war nor peace."
"We must take clear and decisive positions and issue an ultimatum to the countries of the region and the American side in order to create the conditions for breaking the blockade," he said.
IRGC spokesman Hossein Mohabbati also dismissed the possibility of Washington achieving the comprehensive economic blockade it was seeking.
He warned that if Iranian vessels were attacked, "We will strike harder."
US expands enforcement measures against Iranian oil shipments
Washington has tightened enforcement of its naval blockade amid reports that Tehran is preparing to resume oil exports.
Under a new directive issued by US Central Command (CENTCOM), vessels receiving cargo through ship-to-ship transfers from vessels subject to the blockade could be considered to be attempting to evade US restrictions, even if they have never entered Iranian waters.
Such vessels "may be stopped, inspected, diverted or seized," the directive says, which also warns that failure to comply could result in enforcement measures involving the use of force.
The United States reinstated the blockade on July 14.
Since then, US forces have disabled several tankers attempting to reach Kharg Island by firing Hellfire missiles into their engine rooms.
Before the war began in February, Iran exported approximately 1.5 million to 2 million barrels of crude oil per day, with China purchasing most of those shipments.
Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said reopening the Strait of Hormuz would not be difficult if Washington agreed to Tehran's conditions, according to a Saturday report by Tasnim News Agency .
"Reopening the Strait of Hormuz is not difficult, and it is enough for the US to accept reasonable conditions in accordance with Iran's international law," Araghchi said.
Iranian Deputy Foreign Minister Kazem Gharibabadi reaffirmed Araghchi's position after talks with a Qatari delegation in Tehran on Saturday, calling the US economic blockade an act of war and warning that Iran would take all necessary measures to break it.
"We consider the economic blockade (imposed by the American terrorist army) to be an act of war, and we will take any action necessary to break the economic blockade," Gharibabadi told reporters.

items.content:
This Stock Market Selloff Could Block the Fed’s Rate Hikes
Published November 21, 2026, 10:17am ET · 4 min read
This post may contain links from our sponsors and affiliates, and Flywheel Publishing may receive compensation for actions taken through them.
Wooden blocks spelling "FED" sit atop U.S. dollar bills, symbolizing the Federal Reserve's influence on the economy. A percentage cube with arrows suggests the ongoing debate over interest rate movements, a key topic in discussions about monetary policy. © Kenishirotie / Shutterstock.com
The S&P 500 fell 3.70% on Friday and closed at 6,910.39. It was the index's seventh straight loss, and the week's 8.4% decline was its worst since early April 2025. The Nasdaq Composite fell 5.28% to 22,617.73 and is now negative for 2026.
If you own State Street SPDR S&P 500 ETF Trust ( NYSEARCA:SPY ) or Invesco QQQ Trust ( NASDAQ:QQQ ), the selloff raises a question about the Fed. In September, it raised its target range to an upper bound of 4.00% [ 1 ] , and it still looks ready to boost again.
Peter Boockvar, chief investment officer of OnePoint BFG Wealth Partners, posted on X Friday morning about the AI tech selloff and the drop in industrial metals, oil, and fuel prices that followed. If the selloff and the concerns about AI capital spending continue, he said, he does not see how the Fed would boost rates again after December, "if they even do then."
He said he is confident Fed Chair Kevin Warsh is paying attention, but that some of Warsh's colleagues are "not reading the room." He wondered about a December hike only if the selloff continues, and that condition matters for how investors read the weeks before the meeting.
Boockvar's argument depends on how much of the economy is tied to AI. Boockvar estimates that data center spending accounts for about half of U.S. GDP growth.
Boockvar also estimates that AI makes up about half of the S&P 500's market value, and he puts AI's share of S&P 500 earnings growth at about 75%. If his estimates are close, a drop in AI stocks hits the economy in two ways: companies cut data center budgets, and households feel poorer. That concentration is also why the power, cooling, and networking suppliers behind the data centers matter so much. We rounded up seven of them in a free report on AI infrastructure .
He also said upper-income consumers depend on the stock market's wealth effect. When their portfolios contract, richer households spend less. That slows down growth and inflation without any action from the Fed, and cheaper metals and fuel push inflation lower on top of that.
The 2-year Treasury yield follows Fed expectations more closely than any other. It closed Friday at 4.63%, down from 4.88% a week earlier. That 25 basis point weekly drop included 13 basis points on Friday alone, and it matched the fall in the week ended September 6, 2024.
The 10-year yield fell to 4.92% from 5.15%. CME FedWatch still showed about 92% odds of a quarter-point December hike. A falling 2-year yield next to steady December odds means traders still expect a December hike but are pricing in fewer hikes after it.
A Citi note on Friday said markets are signaling that current rates are unsustainably high as stock valuations fall and the risk of slower AI investment grows. The bank still expects a quarter-point hike in December because the Fed wants to protect its inflation credibility. After that, it expects the Fed to hold and to start cutting later in 2027, which matches the path it described on October 14.
Lawrence Gillum of LPL Financial said that if the AI selloff tightens financial conditions more broadly, the Fed can slow down and assess. Fed Governor Lisa Cook disagreed on Friday. She said financial conditions remain too accommodating and that a single hike in September is unlikely to be enough.
QQQ fell 14.8% over the past month, compared with 9.8% for SPY. Chipmakers and chip-equipment companies fill much of QQQ's top holdings, according to its latest SEC filing . Its largest position made up about 7.6% [ 2 ] of net assets at the end of June.
QQQ is now up just 0.58% for the year, and SPY is up 2.26%. The VIX closed Thursday at 28.44 [ 3 ] , close to 30, which usually signals high fear.
SPY spreads its holdings across more sectors than QQQ, so its holders keep some AI exposure without the AI trade deciding all of their returns. QQQ would likely rebound harder than SPY if the Fed stops after December, because lower yields help growth stocks the most, but if concerns about AI spending keep building, QQQ takes more damage, as its larger one-month loss shows. Short-term Treasuries also gain directly from a pause, because their prices rise as yields fall.

Teenager allegedly organised arsons and kidnapping on Signal during Melbourne hospitality wars
Victoria police say boy, 17, communicated with offenders under username ‘Onepercent’
Get our breaking news email , free app or daily news podcast
Victorian police allege a 17-year-old boy tasked others to carry out a series of arsons, home invasions and a mistaken identity kidnapping that resulted in the partial amputation of a victim’s finger during Melbourne’s hospitality wars.
The boy, who was arrested on Friday afternoon, allegedly communicated with the offenders under the username “Onepercent” on the encrypted communications app Signal.
He was charged on Saturday with extortion, making threats to kill, three offences of criminal damage by fire, and home invasion. He was remanded to appear in court later on Saturday.
In a statement, police said it would be alleged that Onepercent was involved in tasking an arson at a York Street, South Melbourne licensed premises on 15 April; two home invasions and a kidnapping four days apart in Springvale later that month; and two arson attacks during March at a Williamstown ice-cream store and a car in Moonee Ponds.
The boy was arrested at a house in the Moonee Ponds region, in Melbourne’s north-west, police said.
Police claim breakthrough in Melbourne’s hospitality wars, alleging links to overseas crime figure
It is alleged a trafficable quantity of cocaine, three phones and cash were seized during the arrest.
Sign up for the Breaking News Australia email Police allege that when the mistaken identity kidnapping occurred at the Springvale property on 22 April, a 34-year-old victim received serious injuries to his lower body and the partial amputation of one of his fingers.
It is alleged the fire at Capriccio Gelateria in Williamstown on 22 March caused $600,000 worth of damage and endangered the lives of residents at the property upstairs.
On 16 November, police appealed for more information about the person behind the Onepercent user name.
“We need the public’s assistance to identify the user of this handle,” Det Insp Graham Banks said at the time.
“There will be people in the wider organised crime network and in our community who will have intimate knowledge of who this person is.
“We are hopeful that those people may now be in a position to come forward and speak to police.”

items.title: Ukraine deals major blow to Putin’s Crimea lifeline, European intel assessment claims - Fox News

items.content:
Putin 'very frustrated' after Ukrainian strikes damage key Kerch Bridge
Fox News contributor Rebeccah Heinrichs says she doubts President Donald Trump's summit with Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin will end the war in Ukraine after Ukrainian strikes hit the Kerch Bridge. She also warns that Trump may be losing patience with Iran as U.S. forces enforce an oil blockade.
Ukraine 's repeated attacks on the Kerch Bridge, one of Russian President Vladimir Putin's most prized infrastructure projects, have dealt a potentially significant blow to Moscow's military supply routes into occupied Crimea, raising questions about Russia's ability to sustain operations as both sides prepare for a difficult winter.
A European intelligence assessment dated Nov. 18 and obtained by Fox News Digital describes Ukraine's latest assault as likely its most successful attack on the heavily defended crossing, following a coordinated campaign targeting Russian air defenses, radar and electronic warfare systems.
Ret. Gen. Philip Breedlove, former NATO Supreme Allied Commander Europe, told Fox News Digital the consequences could extend far beyond the destruction of a symbolic Russian landmark. "The Russians are extremely limited in how they get supplies to Crimea and cutting the Kerch bridge will severely, severely damage their ability to resupply Crimea," Breedlove said.
UKRAINE HITS PUTIN'S PRIZED BRIDGE IN RECORD DRONE BLITZ AS KREMLIN TELLS LAWMAKERS TO PREPARE FOR 'VICTORY'
Ukraine said Monday's strikes destroyed one of the Kerch Strait bridge's two steel arches and the road span that was underneath it. (Security Service of Ukraine)
On Nov. 17, Ukrainian missiles and drones struck the 12-mile bridge linking Russia's Krasnodar region to Crimea, collapsing a major section of the roadway into the Kerch Strait and damaging the adjacent railway.
The crossing, inaugurated by Putin in 2018, has served as both a critical transportation link and a symbol of Russia's annexation of Crimea in 2014.
According to the European intelligence assessment, the attack followed a multiweek Ukrainian operation against Russian defensive systems, intended to weaken the bridge's protection before the main strike.
Ukraine subsequently struck the railway again on Nov.19, temporarily halting train traffic and bringing the number of attacks to three in four days.
The damage has disrupted one of Russia's most direct supply connections to Crimea, which Moscow uses to support military operations in southern Ukraine.
PUTIN LAUNCHES UKRAINE BARRAGE HOURS AFTER TRUMP MEETING AMID ALLEGED RUSSIAN MISSILE BREACH OF NATO AIRSPACE
A view shows the Kerch Bridge linking Russia to Crimea, which was targeted in an explosion by Ukraine on Tuesday, June 3. (Reuters/Alexey Pavlishak)
Russia has developed an alternative land corridor through occupied southern Ukraine, but the European intelligence assessment warns that shifting additional military supplies onto those roads could create significant vulnerabilities.
The assessment identifies slower transportation routes, exposure to Ukrainian drone attacks and pressure on other logistical infrastructure as potential consequences.
Breedlove said Ukraine's campaign should be viewed as an attempt to weaken Russia's hold on the peninsula, rather than simply destroy a bridge. He argued that Russia's options are further constrained by Ukraine's success in challenging Russian naval power in the northern Black Sea.
He pointed out that Ukraine has used maritime and aerial drones to push back Russia's Black Sea Fleet despite lacking large conventional warships.
The European assessment also warns that repairing the bridge could take months. Although limited road traffic might resume within weeks, replacing the collapsed section could take considerably longer, particularly if Ukrainian attacks continue.
Damage above the Kerch–Yenikale Canal could also disrupt shipping between the Black Sea and the Sea of Azov.
UKRAINE'S ATTACKS ON RUSSIA ARE PUSHING PUTIN CLOSER TO NEGOTIATING TABLE, TRUMP NATO AMBASSADOR SAYS
Despite Ukraine's success in striking the bridge, a European intelligence source familiar with Russian strategic assessments offered a pessimistic view of the broader conflict.
"It has more symbolic meaning, but also logistics is paralyzed right now," the source told Fox News Digital, describing the immediate impact of the attacks.
Teenagers are looking at the city view during a partial power outages following Russian attacks in Kyiv on October 31, 2026, amid the Russian invasion of Ukraine. (Tetiana DZHAFAROVA / AFP via Getty Images)
However, the source warned that Moscow is preparing to intensify its winter offensive while using negotiations with Washington to increase political pressure on Kyiv.
"The general trend is not good for Ukraine," the source said.
According to the source, Russia believes it can sustain military pressure long enough to force Ukraine into territorial concessions, particularly in the east.
"They are very convinced that by spring Ukrainians will give up," the source said, describing Moscow's expectations.
Breedlove strongly disputed the assessment that Russia was gaining the upper hand militarily.
"Militarily, the tide is turning against Russia," Breedlove told Fox News Digital, arguing that Russian forces have suffered staggering casualties while making limited battlefield gains.
He said Russian losses in recent months had been extraordinarily high and argued that Moscow's military was failing to achieve significant territorial advances.
Breedlove did, however, acknowledge a distinction between military momentum and the political pressure facing Ukraine.
He suggested that changes in Washington's approach to negotiations could strengthen Putin's position even if Russian forces were struggling on the battlefield.
The competing assessments highlight a central question facing Ukraine: whether its military successes can translate into greater diplomatic leverage before Russia's winter offensive intensifies.
UKRAINE STRIKES 'ONE OF THE LARGEST OIL REFINERIES' IN SOUTHERN RUSSIA AHEAD OF PUTIN-TRUMP MEETING IN CHINA
Russian President Vladimir Putin (C), accompanied with Deputy Prime Minister Dmitry Kozak (L) and head of the Federal Road Agency Roman Starovoyt, points at the map while inspecting the site of the under-construction bridge across the Kerch strait, which will link Russia and the Crimean peninsula, onboard a helicopter, on March 18, 2016. (MIKHAIL KLIMENTYEV/Sputnik/AFP via Getty Images)
Putin has threatened retaliation over the bridge attacks , and on Friday Russia launched a massive missile and drone assault against Ukrainian cities, killing at least eight people, according to Ukrainian authorities.
The strikes came hours after Putin appeared alongside President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping at a summit in China, as Washington continued efforts to advance peace negotiations .
The European intelligence assessment warns that further Ukrainian attacks on the Kerch Bridge during repairs are highly likely, potentially prolonging disruptions to Russian supplies.
Smoke rises in the city during a Russian missile strike, amid Russia's attack on Ukraine, in Kyiv, Ukraine Nov. 20, 2026. (Gleb Garanich/Reuters)
For Moscow, restoring the crossing is now both a logistical challenge and a political priority. For Kyiv, keeping it vulnerable offers a way to increase the cost of Russia's occupation while demonstrating that even Putin's most heavily defended infrastructure remains within reach.
Efrat (Effie) Lachter is a reporter for Fox News Digital with more than 15 years of experience covering conflict , global affairs, human rights and political accountability. She has directed and produced more than 200 documentary segments across more than 40 countries, documenting conflicts, humanitarian crises, corruption, human trafficking, gender-based violence and the human stories behind major world events.
Lachter’s reporting has taken her into conflict zones and crisis areas across the Middle East, Europe, Asia and Africa. Her work has included uncovering human trafficking networks, revealing an ISIS underground torture prison in Syria, documenting the war in Ukraine  and interviewing senior political figures and world leaders. She was also among the Western journalists who entered Russia after the war began to bring testimonies from Putin’s opposition. Lachter is the recipient of the 2022 Peres Center for Peace Award and was a 2023–2024 Knight-Wallace Journalism Fellow at the University of Michigan. She also won two Rockower Awards for Excellence in Reporting. She holds a bachelor's degree in communication and a master's degree in political science.

items.title: US Treasury Secretary Says Nvidia Chip Export Policy to China Holds After Remote-Access Curbs - CASRAI
items.summary: US Treasury Secretary Says Nvidia Chip Export Policy to China Holds After Remote-Access Curbs  CASRAI
items.content:
US Treasury Secretary Says Nvidia Chip Export Policy to China Holds After Remote-Access Curbs
US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent confirmed Nvidia H200 export limits hold after new federal export rules curtailed overseas remote cloud access.
Photo: Carol M. Highsmith / Wikimedia Commons, Public domain (cropped). Source
Following earlier friction where China warned against expanded semiconductor trade barriers , U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent confirmed on November 20, 2026, that current export limits on Nvidia H200 chips will hold without additional restrictions. Speaking after the enactment of a federal interim final rule curbing remote compute access , Bessent stated existing controls are sufficient, providing clarity for university computing clusters and international research compliance offices.
Scott Bessent confirms export threshold holds after remote curbs
Speaking in Washington on November 20, 2026, U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent clarified federal policy regarding advanced semiconductor trade following bilateral diplomatic talks and an official trip to Asia with President Donald Trump. In an interview with CNBC, Bessent declared that the federal government does not plan to impose further restrictions on approved Nvidia artificial intelligence processor exports to commercial buyers in China. Bessent stated that "the proper chip restrictions are in place" and affirmed that "the remote access has been curtailed," as detailed in reporting by Hindustan Times .
Bessent emphasized that executive agencies are prioritizing the enforcement of established thresholds rather than drafting new bans. The confirmation indicates that cleared commercial buyers in China may continue receiving licensed shipments of Hopper-architecture accelerators, including the Nvidia H200, under existing Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) export authorizations, provided they satisfy rigorous end-user verification protocols.
Regulatory provisions, chip volumes, and compute thresholds
The regulatory foundation underpinning Bessent’s announcement is an interim final rule issued by the Commerce Department’s Bureau of Industry and Security titled "Addressing Remote Access to Advanced Semiconductors" (RIN 0694-AK50), published in the Federal Register on November 19, 2026. The rule amended the Export Administration Regulations (EAR) by adding 15 CFR § 744.24, creating a worldwide end-use licensing mandate for data centers providing compute capacity to entities headquartered in Country Group D:5 destinations, including China, or Macau.
Concurrently, congressional committees scrutinized semiconductor export licenses previously granted by federal officials. According to formal committee disclosures released by Chairman Brian Mast of the House Foreign Affairs Committee on November 19, 2026, Commerce Department records indicate that BIS approved 21 export license applications authorizing 879,868 advanced AI processors for Chinese-tied entities through May 11, 2026. These authorizations covered 579,868 Nvidia H200 accelerators and roughly 300,000 comparable AMD Instinct MI325X units, selected from vendor requests exceeding 3.4 million total processors. While marked as approved rather than delivered, the volume underscores the technical scale governed by modern export controls on artificial intelligence hardware .

The BIS rule also instituted a strict knowledge standard for infrastructure providers. Cloud service providers, commercial colocation facilities, and supercomputing operators must document the ownership chain of remote tenants to ensure compute power above the 12 million aggregate TPP threshold is not rented to restricted overseas organizations.
Context of the remote-access loophole and congressional scrutiny
The policy baseline outlined by Bessent addresses an enforcement gap that emerged as physical hardware embargoes intensified. While earlier federal controls halted direct exports of cutting-edge architectures—such as Nvidia’s Blackwell systems—foreign organizations bypassed hardware restrictions by leasing computing capacity remotely through third-country facilities in Southeast Asia and the Middle East.
This bypass mechanism faced intense scrutiny in early November 2026 following corporate changes at Nvidia, including the resignation of chief executive Jensen Huang amid investigations into intermediary supply routes linked to Megaspeed International, a Singapore-based computing firm. Congressional committees initiated inquiries into whether overseas cloud hubs were routing model training cycles to restricted defense entities.
Under statutory authorities codified in the Export Control Reform Act of 2018 , lawmakers accelerated reviews of dual-use licensing standards. The new BIS regulation formally rescinded the previous administration’s AI Diffusion Rule, replacing its global tiers with targeted extraterritorial end-use controls. By addressing the remote-access channel directly through EAR § 744.24, the administration concluded that existing hardware shipment limits on Hopper-tier accelerators are sufficient without cancelling standing commercial licenses.
Reactions from federal agencies, lawmakers, and industry observers
The confirmation that chip export policies will hold drew divergent responses across Washington and the technology sector. Following the release of committee licensing records, a spokesperson for the Bureau of Industry and Security defended the agency’s oversight track record, noting that federal export decisions strictly follow national security criteria published in the Federal Register. As documented in coverage published in Newsday , Commerce officials emphasized that the department maintains transparency with congressional overseers, applying rigorous case-by-case reviews rather than blanket presumptions of denial for older chip tiers.
In Congress, leaders of the House Foreign Affairs Committee voiced contrasting views on the disclosures. Committee Chairman Brian Mast argued that public transparency was necessary to ensure dual-use technologies do not enhance foreign military modernization. Conversely, Ranking Member Gregory Meeks pointed to procedural complexities within the interagency review pipeline, questioning whether evaluations adequately keep pace with the velocity of commercial AI hardware development.
Market analysts and semiconductor industry representatives expressed relief at Bessent’s clarification. The certainty that approved H200 shipments will proceed enables manufacturers to maintain predictable supply lines while reassuring cloud infrastructure providers in approved jurisdictions.
What it means for universities, supercomputing centres, and research offices
For academic research institutions, high-performance computing (HPC) facilities, and sponsored project offices, Bessent’s policy confirmation and the new BIS interim final rule carry direct operational compliance requirements.
First, campus computing centres providing remote access to advanced GPU clusters—specifically systems exceeding the 12 million TPP threshold—must establish identity verification procedures for external users. If academic clusters are shared with foreign visiting scholars or international consortia, export compliance administrators must ensure compute cycles are not provided to organizations affiliated with Country Group D:5 entities without a BIS license. This intersects directly with institutional deemed export regulations , which govern access to technical data and software controls by foreign national researchers in domestic laboratories.
Second, research administrators overseeing cloud compute procurement must verify that overseas facilities comply with destination licensing mandates in newly regulated jurisdictions, specifically Brazil, Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, and Thailand. Sponsored projects utilizing cloud infrastructure in these nations must confirm service providers maintain proper BIS exclusions.
Third, university compliance teams must update their institutional research security compliance programs . Because federal grant agencies require rigorous safeguarding of dual-use hardware, campus export control officers must integrate computing facility audits into standard risk management assessments, ensuring faculty collaborating on multinational AI initiatives remain aligned with federal parameters.
Next steps, regulatory timelines, and oversight milestones
The regulatory framework announced by the administration sets in motion several critical milestones. Because the BIS interim final rule took effect immediately upon Federal Register publication on November 19, 2026, export compliance officers and data center operators must adjust operational workflows immediately.
The Commerce Department has opened a 60-day public comment period on RIN 0694-AK50, inviting input from cloud providers, academic institutions, and semiconductor manufacturers until January 19, 2027. This consultation window offers research universities an opportunity to seek formal administrative guidance on how the 12 million aggregate TPP threshold applies to academic collaborative research and non-profit computing consortia.
Data centers delivering compute capacity above the controlled threshold to covered entities have a 90-day transition window to file for necessary export licenses or adjust tenant arrangements. Meanwhile, Capitol Hill will maintain active oversight: the Senate Banking Committee and the House Foreign Affairs Committee have scheduled hearings for December 2026 to examine semiconductor supply chains, agency license approvals, and interagency coordination between Treasury and Commerce.

items.summary: All options open in future talks, says Ed Miliband, while prime minister hails ‘a good day for Britain and Europe’The UK rejoining the EU could be on the table in informal discussions between Andy Burnham and European leaders in Brussels, Ed Miliband has said.The foreign secretary said “all options” would be examined in the process, after the prime minister agreed deals on trade and young people with the bloc on Friday. <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/politics/2026/nov/
items.content:
Ed Miliband (left) with first secretary of state, Louise Haigh, and Andy Burnham at the EU Council in Brussels on Friday. Photograph: Hannah McKay/AFP/Getty
Ed Miliband (left) with first secretary of state, Louise Haigh, and Andy Burnham at the EU Council in Brussels on Friday. Photograph: Hannah McKay/AFP/Getty
Rejoining EU ‘on the table’ as UK makes deals on trade and young people
All options open in future talks, says Ed Miliband, while prime minister hails ‘a good day for Britain and Europe’
The UK rejoining the EU could be on the table in informal discussions between Andy Burnham and European leaders in Brussels, Ed Miliband has said.
The foreign secretary said “all options” would be examined in the process, after the prime minister agreed deals on trade and young people with the bloc on Friday.
Agreements on food and drink standards, emissions trading and a youth mobility scheme were announced after talks this week. Under the plans, 100,000 young Britons will be allowed to live, work, study and travel in the EU, with similar access for Europeans in the UK.
Burnham said the agreement would add 0.5% to the UK’s GDP, a £17bn boost to the British economy.
Miliband said Burnham would have further “brainstorming” discussions with the EU in the next year about what could happen next. He said the agreements this week were the limit of what could be done before the next general election.
Andy, António and Ursula: the joyful EU throuple break Nigel’s bitter heart | John Crace
However, the trio of deals could be derailed in six months, as the EU threatened to block them unless the UK allows European students to pay domestic-level fees to study at British universities.
Miliband said in an interview for the BBC’s Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg that “all the options will be on the table” when pressed on whether rejoining the bloc would be considered, adding: “We will look at the benefits and the costs of all the different options.”
Since entering government in 2024, Labour has stuck to the “red lines” in its manifesto, which stated the party would not rejoin the single market or customs union. It also ruled out freedom of movement.
Burnham has previously said he wants to see the UK rejoin the EU in his lifetime.
The prime minister will use the announcement of his 10-year plan before Christmas to explore how the UK could get closer to the EU after the next election. Informal discussions will take place with Brussels before next year’s UK-EU summit.
Miliband said he accepts the result of the 2016 vote but “the world has changed massively”.
“Europe is changing too, so we’ve got to look at what that means,” he said. “It’s not about this parliament, we’re respecting the red lines in this parliament.”
Misty-eyed Burnham gambles on closer ties with EU as he throws down gauntlet to Tories and Reform
He also denied the deal with the EU would rely on progress in discussions on students from the bloc coming to the UK. It has been reported that a proposal from the bloc to lower the level of tuition fees paid by EU students in the UK has not been agreed.
Miliband told the BBC it was “absolutely clear” the agreements on food exports, energy and youth mobility would apply, even though there has not been a deal on tuition fees.
The foreign secretary said: “The dates are set out in 2028 when these things are coming in, we’re introducing legislation in parliament, so definitely.”
On Friday, Burnham said the agreement represented a “good day for Britain and Europe”. He said the agreements answer “the biggest challenges of our times and the biggest worries that people have”, citing the cost of living, lack of economic growth, illegal immigration and challenges facing young people.
“The deal is done. It is there in black and white in front of you,” Burnham said, adding that the legislation would enter parliament next week.
The European Commission president, Ursula von der Leyen, played down the disagreement, saying she was “confident we are going to find a solution”. About the further discussions, she said: “We welcome this brainstorming, so count on us.”
The environment secretary, Angela Eagle, told BBC Radio 4’s Today programme on Saturday the deal was good for farmers. “(It) will open up new markets. They’ll be able to import and expor. This is a win-win for the UK. We will dissolve a lot of the friction and costs at the border for UK agriculture and food.”

Thanksgiving Gas Prices Could Break a Record Despite Recent Plunge
Gasoline prices have fallen nearly 60 cents in a month, but Americans heading out for Thanksgiving could still pay more at the pump than during any previous Thanksgiving.
The national average fell to $3.69 per gallon on Friday, according to AAA , down from approximately $4.30 a month ago. GasBuddy expects prices to average $3.62 on Thanksgiving Day, which would surpass the previous holiday record of $3.56 set in 2022.
The declines are substantial. Gasoline prices have been falling for weeks as crude oil prices retreat and supplies recover from the disruptions caused by the Iran war. West Texas Intermediate crude fell into the low $80s this week, while U.S. gasoline inventories increased by 5.1 million barrels to 215.9 million barrels.
Seasonal factors are helping, too. Refineries have switched to less expensive winter-blend gasoline, and demand typically declines after the summer driving season.
Americans are still paying roughly 60 cents more per gallon than they were a year ago. For a 500-mile round trip in a vehicle averaging 25 miles per gallon, that's approximately $12 more in gasoline costs than last November, despite the recent price declines.
AAA expects 72.9 million Americans to travel by car over Thanksgiving, down from 73.1 million last year. GasBuddy's holiday survey found that nearly one in five drivers plans to reduce other holiday spending to cover fuel costs.
Flying isn't offering much relief. AAA expects nearly 6 million Americans to travel by air, with domestic round-trip tickets booked through its service averaging $800, up 17% from last Thanksgiving. Elevated jet fuel costs have contributed to higher airfares.
Diesel remains expensive as well, averaging approximately $5.90 per gallon Thursday. Those costs affect trucking and agriculture, with the American Farm Bureau Federation reporting that Thanksgiving dinner prices have increased 6% this year.
Gasoline prices may continue falling before Thursday. Whether they fall enough to avoid a Thanksgiving record remains uncertain, particularly with Middle Eastern tanker traffic still facing attacks despite the recovery in crude exports.

The AI bust is a growing threat to China’s economy and a ‘moment of real danger’ for President Xi Jinping, analyst warns
Chinese President Xi Jinping walks out to receive U.S. President Donald Trump for a bilateral meeting at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) Economic Leaders' Meeting on November 16, 2026 in Shenzhen, China. Carlos Barria-China Pool/Getty Images
U.S. investors are facing a meltdown in tech stocks and the possible end of the AI boom, but the bubble has already popped in China, where an even worse market crash threatens the economy and President Xi Jinping, according to Yardeni Research.
China’s tech-heavy STAR 50 index has tumbled 44% from its high this summer, while the Nasdaq is down 18% from its record—even after U.S. stocks suffered their worst week since the early days of the COVID-19 pandemic.
That’s thrown a wrench into Xi’s plans for the economy, Yardeni said in a note earlier this month. While the Chinese leader was riding high as host to global leaders this week, the market’s downturn jeopardizes his plan to turn China’s savers into stock investors who can finance the AI buildout and de-emphasize the property market.
Real estate accounts for roughly 70% of household wealth in China and was traditionally a place to stash savings. But the housing crash has weighed on consumer demand, even producing intermittent deflation. Business investment is also falling, with October data showing property investment sank nearly 22%.
With the domestic market still weak, Beijing has instead relied on a flood of cheap exports to keep the economy growing while also deploying the “national team” of state-backed banks to pump money into the stock market.
But according to Yardeni, Chinese stocks collapsed this year due in part to cutthroat competition, heavier tax burdens, higher energy costs, tariffs, and the risk that China’s trading partners will block exports being sold at ultra-low prices.
“To keep AI funding flowing, Xi needs a buoyant stock market,” the note said. “Otherwise, AI risks being folded into the state-owned enterprise (SOE) universe that his team has pledged to shrink since 2013, further crowding out the private sector.”
Retail investors are also skittish about Chinese stocks after Xi’s government cracked down on the tech sector in 2020. The market’s reputation as a rigged casino that favors politically connected insiders doesn’t help either. In fact, the Shanghai Composite remains well below its October 2007 peak despite China’s GDP exploding nearly sixfold.
Many households now have “financial PTSD” after repeated stock busts, including a crash in the summer of 2015 that required an aggressive national team rescue, Yardeni added.
To be sure, China remains a leader in AI, and mom-and-pop investors still drive most of the trade, even as they treat the market more like high-stakes gambling than a place to grow retirement savings.
“Yet this is a moment of real danger for Xi. A bursting AI bubble would not merely erase wealth or dent China’s technological prestige. It would weaken Beijing’s attempt to replace a broken property model with a stock-market-led one,” Yardeni warned.
“China can build world-class AI models, train engineers, and spend billions on chips. But if its households still view Shanghai as a casino with odds set by the Politburo, Xi’s dream of creating a Chinese version of Wall Street may remain just that: a dream.”
Underscoring its importance to Beijing, Premier Li Qiang told a State Council executive meeting earlier this month that stabilizing capital markets was the top priority for the rest of the year.
It followed securities regulators sharply easing requirements for company buybacks that help lift stock prices and discouraging IPOs and large share sales to prevent stock dilution that triggers selloffs.
But the spy scandal that dethroned Jensen Huang as CEO of Nvidia represents a new risk to China’s AI ambitions. Backlash over the advanced U.S. chips and computing capacity that China had access to has spurred the Trump administration to impose new technology curbs.
“By targeting both indirect chip shipments to China and its access to overseas computing power, the new controls threaten to slow the catch-up of China’s leading AI models and to slow China’s AI rollout,” analysts at Capital Economics wrote on Tuesday.

items.title: Trafalgar Square Christmas tree felled in Norway
items.summary: The 21m tree is Oslo’s annual thank you for Britain’s support during World War Two.
items.content:
Image caption, Karen Scarborough (left) and Anne Lindboe got to work with a two-handled saw
This year's Trafalgar Square Christmas tree has been cut down in a forest outside Oslo, ready to begin its journey to London.
The 21m (69ft) tree, nicknamed Jolly Cheery, is about 75 years old. It was felled on Friday by the Lord Mayor of Westminster, Karen Scarborough, and the Mayor of Oslo, Anne Lindboe.
Norway has sent a tree to the capital every year since 1947 as a thank you for Britain's support during World War Two, when King Haakon VII and the Norwegian government lived in exile in London.
Its lights will be switched on by the two mayors at a ceremony in the square on Thursday, 3 December.
Scarborough said: "It's my greatest honour to take part in this wonderful tradition for both the cities of Oslo and London.
"This tree is a powerful symbol of friendship and peace, reminding us to be there for one another during the festive period."
Image caption, The 21m tree has been nicknamed Jolly Cheery
Scarborough thanked "the people of Oslo and Norway for this truly fabulous gift" and added: "With the care and dedication of the team, I'm sure it will look magnificent on Trafalgar Square."
Lindboe said: "Oslo has been sending a Christmas tree to London for almost eight decades, and every year we send a tree across the North Sea with the same message: we have not forgotten.
"The tradition has a powerful history, and its message remains just as relevant today.
"I hope Jolly Cheery spreads warmth and Christmas cheer to everyone who passes by, and reminds us how much it means to be there for one another, especially in difficult times."
Image caption, Count the rings: Anne Lindboe (left) and Karen Scarborough (right) with a slice of the 75-year-old trunk
For the second year running, the tree was chosen with the help of a social media poll.
Organisers said it would travel by road in Norway and England using only electric and biodiesel vehicles, cutting the journey's carbon footprint by 80%. It will cross the North Sea on a regular cargo ship from the port of Brevik.
Once in London, it will be decorated in the traditional Norwegian style, with 25m strings of festoon lighting fitted with energy-efficient bulbs.

items.title: Vance stops short of endorsing Trump’s claim that Iran was close to nuclear weapon - The Guardian
items.summary: Vance stops short of endorsing Trump’s claim that Iran was close to nuclear weapon  The Guardian
items.content:
JD Vance, with Marco Rubio and Donald Trump, at a news conference in the White House on Friday. Photograph: Jacquelyn Martin/AP
JD Vance, with Marco Rubio and Donald Trump, at a news conference in the White House on Friday. Photograph: Jacquelyn Martin/AP
Vance stops short of endorsing Trump’s claim that Iran was close to nuclear weapon
US vice-president says it’s not his place to second-guess the president, but refrains from endorsing Trump’s claim
At a White House news conference on Friday, JD Vance stopped short of endorsing Donald Trump’s claim that Iran was so close to obtaining a nuclear weapon in February that it was essential for the US to go to war with the Islamic republic.
In the White House briefing room, Trump was asked about reporting this week that he was unhappy with the US vice-president’s statement blaming Republican losses in the midterm elections on the Iran war.
“I didn’t say I was unhappy with it,” Trump said. “I thought the statement was fine, except I would have had one other thing, that if it were asked, I would have said that: ‘Would you do it again?’ And absolutely, the answer is yes, because we cannot allow Iran to have a nuclear weapon.”
However, Trump’s claim that Iran was so close to developing a nuclear weapon this year that it was necessary to go to war, which he has made dozens of times in the past nine months, is undermined by public evidence and contradicts his own previous statements on US strikes against Iranian facilities in 2025.
At a campaign rally in Alaska last month, Trump insisted that he had to join Israel in attacking Iran in February because, “they were two weeks away from having a nuclear weapon”.
That claim appears at odds with what his then director of national intelligence, Tulsi Gabbard, testified to Congress on 25 March 2025, two months into Trump’s second term: that US intelligence agencies reported that Iran had not tried to make a nuclear weapon for more than two decades. The US intelligence community, Gabbard said, “continues to assess Iran is not building a nuclear weapon and supreme leader Khamenei has not authorized the nuclear weapons program he suspended in 2003”.
Despite that assessment, three months later, on 21 June 2025, Trump ordered the US bombing of Iran’s nuclear enrichment facilities. The strikes, Trump told the public that night , “were a spectacular military success. Iran’s key nuclear enrichment facilities have been completely and totally obliterated.”
Eight months after that, however, when Trump announced the start of a full-scale war on Iran early on 28 February 2026, he said in a video statement from Mar-a-Lago the war was necessary to “ensure that Iran does not obtain a nuclear weapon”.
The morning after this month’s midterm elections, Vance said in a statement posted on social media: “The reason we lost is the war.”
“If you’d like to argue it was worth it, that losing the Senate for the next 6 years was worth it, then do so,” he added. “Argue it was a worthwhile cost to pay. Agree or disagree, that’s at least honest. But everyone knows why we lost.”
In the White House briefing room on Friday, after Trump said that Vance should have said the war was necessary, a reporter asked the vice-president whether he would argue that the war in Iran was worth it.
In his response, Vance said it was not his place to second-guess the president, but refrained from actually endorsing Trump’s claim that the war was essential to stop Iran from creating a nuclear weapon.
“Look, what I’ve said is the goal of keeping Iran from getting a nuclear weapon is absolutely what we need to be doing. It’s the biggest state sponsor of terrorism. If they had a nuclear weapon, they would use it as leverage or, God forbid, they would attack and kill thousands, hundreds of thousands, of innocent people,” Vance said. “I think the president is the one who makes the decision, and the president has said he would do it again.”
“My view is that my goal is, and my job is, to support the president of the United States,” the vice-president said.
The vice president’s office did not respond to a request to comment.

items.content:
Iran unveils underground 'missile city,' claims it struck US F-16 over Persian Gulf
Iran unveils underground 'missile city,' claims it struck US F-16 over Persian Gulf
Iran unveiled an underground missile facility and claimed it struck a US F-16, a report Washington has not confirmed; Tehran also demanded US commitments before reopening the Strait of Hormuz amid stalled negotiations
Iran's military claimed Saturday that its air defenses struck a U.S. F-16 fighter jet over the Persian Gulf on Friday evening, forcing it to abort its mission and make an emergency landing at a nearby airport. The U.S. military has not confirmed the claim.
The report came amid escalating tensions in the Middle East and the possibility of renewed strikes on Iran. On Friday, Tehran unveiled what it described as an underground "missile city," warning: "There are surprises. There will be no hesitation in using force." Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi also set conditions for resuming negotiations, demanding that Washington fulfill its commitments before Iran reopens the Strait of Hormuz.
Majid Mousavi, commander of the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps' Aerospace Force, visited the new facility and said: "The Aerospace Force is ready and prepared to carry out the supreme leader's orders across all operational theaters. Our aerospace capabilities have expanded significantly in the period between the conflicts. Highly effective systems have been developed that strengthen deterrence."
Iranian officials claim the facility is new, but they made a similar announcement earlier this month, leaving it unclear whether the footage reflects the restoration of military capabilities or Iranian propaganda intended to unsettle the United States and Israel.
Iranian media quoted IRGC commander Ahmad Vahidi as saying: "What is happening to the enemy now is only the beginning. You will witness the enemy's humiliation and complete defeat. Truth will prevail over falsehood." Iranian reports claimed the remarks were made inside the facility shown in the footage.
Iran's demands for reopening the Strait of Hormuz
Responding to President Donald Trump's statement that "they want to make a deal, but they don't want to make a deal that's acceptable to me," Araghchi said the Islamic Republic would accept any timetable for an agreement, provided its demands were met.
"The Islamabad memorandum of understanding is no longer on the table and has no binding force," he clarified.
Oil tanker strikes naval mines in the Strait of Hormuz
He also referred to a proposal Iran presented during negotiations in late October to reopen the Strait of Hormuz within two days if Washington met Tehran's demands.
"Our current position is that the two-day plan remains on the table if the Americans are serious about reaching an agreement. If they want to shorten the timetable from two days to one day, or even two hours, that is not a problem. What matters is that our demands are met," he said.
Araghchi said that under such circumstances, the United States would first have to "fulfill specific commitments," after which Iran would reopen the Strait of Hormuz . These steps, he said, would "pave the way for negotiations toward a final agreement."
The Iranian foreign minister also emphasized that Tehran has two red lines regarding its nuclear material.
"We have two red lines on this issue. The first is that these materials will not leave the country. The second is that they will be used according to our needs."
Araghchi said the current state of "neither war nor peace must end," adding that only two options remained: peace or war.
"The countries of the region have learned important lessons from this war, the most important being that they cannot rely on outside powers to guarantee their security. Mediators are moving between us and the United States, delivering and receiving messages and presenting various ideas and proposals. There are economic exchanges between us and the countries of the region. We are diplomats, and we place our hopes in diplomacy."
Meanwhile, the IRGC Navy announced that an oil tanker "operating in violation of regulations and with the backing of the U.S. military attempted to pass through an unauthorized route" and struck naval mines in the Strait of Hormuz, triggering an explosion and fire.
Following the announcement, the Revolutionary Guards released footage of the explosion and issued a warning: "We are monitoring every movement of every vessel that violates regulations in the Strait of Hormuz and the Persian Gulf."
Iran's Tasnim news agency reported: "According to operational reports received, the U.S. military attempted Thursday night to facilitate the unauthorized transfer of cargo and the smuggling of fuel through the Strait of Hormuz. During these operations, explosions and intense fires were documented aboard oil tankers in the southern sector of the Strait of Hormuz.
"The first incident occurred near the port of Khasab, and the second took place early Friday morning off the coast of Ghanam Island. According to the IRGC Navy spokesperson, the explosions were caused by the vessels involved striking naval mines."
Tasnim also claimed that Iran's air defense system had destroyed an American MQ-9 drone "responsible for conducting surveillance and providing air cover for the operation west of the Strait of Hormuz."
Iranian media footage showing an alternative route bypassing the B1 bridge in Karaj
Iranian media also reported the opening of an alternative route to the B1 bridge connecting Tehran and Karaj, which was struck twice during Operation Roaring Lion.
'They don't want to make a deal that's acceptable to me'
U.S. President Donald Trump held a news conference at the White House on Thursday, a day after returning to the United States from the historic trilateral summit in China.
Addressing Iran, Trump linked gasoline prices to the outcome of negotiations with Tehran, saying the two countries had yet to reach terms acceptable to him. He said Washington wanted "a real deal, not a fake deal" and accused Iran of "bullshitting people for 51 years."
Trump continued: "We talked extensively about ensuring that Iran will never have a nuclear weapon. They're crazy. We're not going to let them have a nuclear weapon. Iran, I say it, I'll say it now — and I'm not George Bush — watch my lips. No, you don't have to watch my lips. Iran will never have a nuclear weapon, ever."
During the news conference, Trump was asked about reports that Iran was developing plans to potentially detonate a "dirty bomb" in Washington, D.C.
"There is a rumor that they're building a dirty bomb. If they do, we're going to find— we know a lot about what's happening in Iran. We know everything they say. We know who they are, where they are. We'll find out about it. We will not allow that to happen."
Trump did not address reports of mediation efforts between the United States and Iran.
About a week earlier, Trump declared that "we don't need a deal with Iran" and directed Vice President JD Vance to shift his focus away from negotiations with Tehran. "Those days have long since passed," Trump wrote, adding: "We've got their money, Hundreds of Billions of Dollars, and we've got their Strait!"

items.content:
As the market leader with high prices, Nvidia could see margins compress if AI chips become more commoditized.
Cheaper chips and more alternatives would be good news for TSMC.
With cheaper price points, Alphabet and AMD should benefit from chip fungibility.
The AI chip market is starting to shift, and with it, Nvidia 's ( NVDA -14.01% ) grip. Anthropic recently revealed that its Claude Mythos model could start running part of its AI models on alternative AI chips to Nvidia's graphics processing units (GPUs) in just a few days with basically no human intervention, a process that used to take six to 12 months and dozens of engineers. This greatly reduces Nvidia's CUDA moat at a time when competitors are starting to catch up.
Alphabet 's ( GOOGL -2.70% ) ( GOOG -2.59% ) Tensor Processing Units (TPUs) have started to outperform Nvidia's GPUs on a performance-per-dollar basis, according to Semianalysis (though some dispute the results). Meanwhile, Advanced Micro Devices ' ( AMD -13.25% ) GPUs continue to gain traction. The company has improved its software stack, and its chips' larger memory capacity makes them ideal for inference.
If the gap between AI chips continues to shrink and AI models can be quickly shifted to run on any AI accelerator, this is very bad news for Nvidia. Not only will the company continue to lose market share, but, more importantly, its pricing power will erode, and its margins will shrink. The Nvidia premium can be seen in its gross margins , which are in the mid-70% range, versus AMD’s in the mid-50% range. Meanwhile, all of Nvidia's largest customers, outside of SpaceX ( SPCX -7.69% ) , have been developing their own custom AI chips to try to break free of Nvidia's high prices.

All is not lost for Nvidia, as the company still holds some advantages. It has created a cohesive hardware, software, and networking ecosystem that should still be able to command a premium. It also has major current supply chain advantages, having locked up more access to constrained high bandwidth memory (HBM) supply and having more manufacturing and packaging capacity with Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing ( TSM -9.48% ) . That will help it maintain its leadership position, even as it will likely face continued market-share and pricing pressure.
While Nvidia may struggle, these three AI stocks look set to benefit.

Lower AI accelerator prices and more Nvidia GPU alternatives could boost overall AI chip demand, which would benefit Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing. It would also lower TSMC's customer concentration and could actually help with pricing power and gross margins.
Whether a hyperscaler, neocloud, enterprise, or government buys Nvidia GPUs, AMD accelerators, or ASICs through a company like Broadcom ( AVGO -12.19% ) or Marvell Technology ( MRVL -11.69% ) , TSMC still wins at the end of the day. That makes the stock a buy.

As both a cloud computing giant and a developer of TPUs, Alphabet is one of the best-positioned companies to benefit from the commoditization of AI chips. Alphabet has more than a decade's head start with custom chips and is creating an ecosystem to rival chipmakers like Nvidia and AMD. This lets it get better utilization out of its data centers and gives it an advantage over other companies using their own custom AI chips.
Meanwhile, because its offerings cost much less than Nvidia's, it should be able to gain share with external customers without sacrificing margins. This ultimately could make Alphabet one of the biggest winners in the AI space during this transition.
Starting from a much smaller market-share base with an operating model already built around slimmer gross margins, AMD should benefit as AI chips become more commoditized. Between its lower prices, improving cost performance, and the recent introduction of a complete AI rack system (Helios), AI chip pricing normalization and chip fungibility actually become a tailwind rather than a headwind for a smaller Nvidia competitor like AMD.
Meanwhile, the market is heading in AMD's direction with inference and agentic AI, with customers caring far more about memory capacity, central processing unit (CPU) integrations, and cost-per-action, which is where its chips shine. With its new Helios system, which combines its GPUs and CPUs, AMD has a big opportunity to establish itself as a meaningful alternative to Nvidia in the coming years. This makes the stock a buy.

The semiconductor industry is experiencing a sell-off, and even some of the sector's leaders, including Advanced Micro Devices (NASDAQ:AMD) and Nvidia (NASDAQ:NVDA), haven't escaped the bloodbath. Both companies have faced headwinds in recent weeks and have lost significant market value as a result. AMD's shares have dropped 21% over the past month, while Nvidia's are down 40%. Which of these two stocks is a better buy right now?
Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue »
AMD was the subject of a short-seller report by Hunterbrook Media alleging that the semiconductor leader may have violated export restrictions, since some of its firmware ended up at a blacklisted Chinese server manufacturer. However, Hunterbrook Media itself acknowledges that it doesn't know whether AMD itself supplied the software.
Meanwhile, Reuters has said it couldn't independently verify these claims, while AMD has denied them. So, this may be a giant nothingburger, after all. Yet, the stock fell because of the short-seller report, which arguably creates an attractive entry point.
AMD is capitalizing on the agentic AI boom, thanks to its market-leading CPU (central processing unit) servers. Third-quarter revenue jumped 45% year over year to $13.4 billion, while data center revenue soared 97% year over year to $8.5 billion.
AMD's non-GAAP earnings per share (EPS) were $2.09, up 74% compared to the year-ago period. AMD sees its revenue jump by more than 80% in 2027, while it expects its server CPU total addressable market to grow at a compound annual rate of more than 50% and reach $220 billion by 2030. That paints a very bright picture for the company's future.
Nvidia is going through a transition. The company's co-founder and longtime CEO, Jensen Huang, was involved in a scandal involving extramarital affairs, including with an alleged Chinese spy.
Huang stepped down as a result, a big blow to the company, given what he had built up to that point. Nvidia's board has appointed its CFO, Colette Kress, as interim CEO while it continues its search for its next leader. Despite all that mess, the company's financial results remain excellent.
In the third quarter of its fiscal year 2027, which ended on Oct. 25, Nvidia's revenue increased by 103% year over year to $115.8 billion. The company's data center revenue soared 110% year over year to $107.6 billion.
Nvidia's non-GAAP EPS was $2.68, up 111% year over year. Nvidia's quarterly update blew past expectations, and its guidance was impressive as well. The semiconductor leader expects $130 billion in revenue (at the midpoint) in its upcoming fourth quarter, representing an almost 91% year-over-year increase. And Nvidia expects its revenue to grow about 75% year over year in its fiscal year 2028, which will cover most of the calendar year 2027.
The loss of Huang is a problem, but Nvidia has many advantages that remain intact, including technological expertise, deep relationships with many corporations it does business with, and its CUDA ecosystem, which provides a wide moat from switching costs. With the right leader at the helm, it could still beat the market over the long run.
Nvidia currently generates higher revenue and profits, and is growing both metrics faster.
It also boasts higher gross margins. However, Nvidia's search for a new CEO introduces significant uncertainty. AMD's short-seller-related problems aren't nearly as dire, in my view.
Further, AMD's revenue growth is accelerating, particularly within its all-important data center segment, while Nvidia's revenue growth could decline next year. Does that make AMD the better buy?
We'd need to look at valuation as well, and in that category, Nvidia is the winner, as seen in their respective price-to-earnings (P/E) ratios above. Nvidia might be facing tougher headwinds right now, but the market has adjusted for that by giving the company much lower valuation multiples. Nvidia is far too cheap at current levels, in my view, and while I'd also buy AMD's shares right now, Nvidia's look even more attractive.

The AI sell-off now has Taiwan taking emergency steps to calm its chip-heavy market
Taiwanese financial regulators are taking drastic steps to calm the country's markets.
Taiwan's Financial Supervisory Commission said it was limiting short selling in local markets.
The move comes on the heels of an intense market sell-off in AI and tech.
Financial regulators in Taiwan said they would limit short selling in local markets effective Monday, a move that could further rattle investors during an intense tech stock sell-off .
In a statement on Saturday, Taiwan's Financial Supervisory Commission said it was taking the action "in response to the recent significant fluctuations in the Taiwan stock market."
Taiwan's main trading index, which is heavily weighted toward semiconductor stocks, fell 17.5% over the last five trading days.
In US markets, the S&P 500 and the Dow entered correction territory on Friday, meaning they had fallen at least 10% from recent highs.
Some market pros have pointed to the week's stock market carnage to predict that the AI trade is at a turning point, possibly on its last legs as a host of headwinds reshape the outlook.
Michael Burry , the investor made famous by "The Big Short," reminded investors on Thursday that he's been sounding the alarm about chip makers and neoclouds for some time now.
"Coreweave, Nebius, Nvidia, semis, I tried to warn you all," he wrote on X. "I didn't say short. But I provided the information one would need to sell."
Taiwanese regulators said the limits comprised "a complete ban on short selling below the closing price."
"This does not apply to short selling and borrowing by securities firms and futures companies for hedging purposes," their statement said.
The limits on short-selling would hobble investors looking to hedge. To raise cash, they might sell their long positions.
In 2008, the US Securities and Exchange Commission temporarily banned short selling for a slew of financial stocks during the collapse of the housing market.
The intervention largely failed to ease the decline. Then SEC Chairman Christopher Cox said in a press release announcing the measure that it "would not be necessary in a well-functioning market."

Thousands of people have taken to the streets across Europe to protest against rising living costs, unaffordable housing and cuts to public services, as students and workers demand action from their governments.
Demonstrators marched across France and Portugal on Saturday, following youth-led protests in several European countries on Friday.

The gatherings reflect overlapping concerns about economic insecurity, education and future opportunities, although their demands and scale differ considerably between countries.
In France, the Ministry of Interior said 82,500 people joined demonstrations nationwide on Saturday, including 21,500 in Paris, down from 106,000 the previous weekend. Organisers estimated a higher turnout of 150,000.
The protests, now in their sixth consecutive weekend, began in September with students demanding better schools before expanding to include trade unions and the Yellow Vests, a movement that emerged in 2018 over rising fuel prices and living costs.
Demonstrators have also criticised police violence and a new law strengthening protections for officers who use firearms.
People react ahead of a protest in Paris, France, on November 21, 2026, the sixth consecutive Saturday of demonstrations against the high cost of living and police violence. The Yellow Vests organised the protest, and high school and university students joined to demand better conditions in schools and universities [Gonzalo Fuentes/Reuters] Portugal protests
In Portugal, thousands marched through Lisbon despite heavy rain, calling for higher wages, affordable housing and relief from rising prices.
The demonstration was organised by CGTP, the country’s largest trade union federation, which also demanded higher pensions and cheaper essential goods.
Portugal’s housing pressures have intensified as property prices have more than doubled since 2017.
Average annual earnings in 2025 were 37 percent below the European Union average, according to the EU’s statistics agency, Eurostat.
The weekend’s demonstrations followed Friday’s youth protests in Germany and Sweden.
About 4,000 people gathered in Berlin, while police reported roughly 200 participants at a Saturday march in Helsinki organised by left-wing and student groups.
Organisers of an international youth strike said demonstrations were planned in at least 25 countries, with demands ranging from greater education funding and climate action to opposition to compulsory military service.
People raise their fists and sing during a trade union protest against the government’s proposed budget in Lisbon, Portugal, on November 21, 2026 [Armando Franca/AP Photo] In Germany, the youth campaign Gen Z regelt, meaning “Generation Z takes charge”, announced demonstrations in 73 locations.
In Italy, a nationwide strike organised by the CGIL, one of the country’s main trade union confederations, disrupted transport, schools and some healthcare services on Friday.
Demonstrations took place in more than 100 cities, with union leader Maurizio Landini claiming more than one million participants nationwide.
While some protests were linked through the international youth initiative, others grew out of established national campaigns, bringing different groups onto the streets over concerns about living standards and government spending.
Separately, thousands protested in the Croatian capital, Zagreb, on Saturday over the death of a man at a psychiatric hospital.

items.title: Killer robots: U.N. talks fall short of hopes for legally binding rules
items.summary: U.N. talks in Geneva have failed to deliver binding rules on autonomous weapons, as humanitarian groups warn that military AI is advancing far faster than diplomacy.
items.content:
Killer robots: The race to control weapons that can decide who lives or dies U.N. talks in Geneva have failed to deliver binding rules on autonomous weapons, as humanitarian groups warn that military AI is advancing far faster than diplomacy.
Killer robots: U.N. talks fall short of hopes for legally binding rules
A Ukrainian FP-1 long-range attack drone is launched at an undisclosed location in Ukraine, Aug. 16, 2026.
GENEVA — Diplomats meeting at the United Nations in Geneva have agreed to start discussing options to regulate lethal autonomous weapons, often called "killer robots."
After a week of negotiations that dragged on until the small hours of Saturday morning, a compromise emerged: countries would have two years to suggest regulations that could be legally binding, but could also be optional.
Bleary-eyed negotiators insisted the agreement was better than nothing and showed the U.N.'s disarmament process could still function. But for many humanitarian organizations and many countries, the deal falls far short of what they had hoped for.
Before the negotiations got underway, the International Committee of the Red Cross, the guardian of the Geneva Conventions, said it was urgent for legally binding rules to be drafted within a year. That call was backed by the U.N. secretary-general and by Pope Leo .
Their concerns stem from the kind of warfare we are now seeing. In Ukraine, Sudan and Gaza, civilians are being killed by semi-autonomous drones. This year in Sudan , 80% of civilian deaths were caused by drones according to the U.N.
Besieged Sudanese city faces relentless drone strikes and risk of mass atrocities, U.N. warns
Humans remain, albeit very remotely, in control for now, but humanitarian organizations fear we are on the verge of seeing artificial intelligence-assisted weapons make the decision to kill entirely on their own.
"There is a fundamental ethical concern with having what are essentially these life-and-death decisions determined by programming, determined by an algorithm," said ICRC legal adviser Georgia Hinds. "That's not something that you can fix with better technology. That is a moral red line that we cannot cross."
No one went into the negotiations thinking they would be easy; some of the world's most powerful countries, among them the U.S., Russia and Israel, had already indicated their reluctance to agree to binding regulations.
On day one, Russia delayed proceedings by objecting to the meeting's agenda. Then the United States proposed a five-year window to discuss nonbinding, optional guidelines for autonomous weapons.
How AI drones are influencing the course of the Ukraine war
"They're just kicking the can down the road," said one frustrated delegate. As the clock ticked on and the weekend approached, diplomats scrambled to get some kind of result from negotiations that had been billed as a last chance to regulate weapons whose technology and decision-making capabilities we may not even fully understand.
Finally, at 4:30 a.m. on Saturday morning, they emerged from the negotiating room to announce their compromise: no to a deal within a year, maybe to legally binding rules, or maybe not.
The ICRC immediately said it regretted the move and renewed its appeal for a binding treaty. Other campaigners were less polite, calling the deal "a real disappointment" and a "nothing burger." "I am concerned people will die because of this," added another.
A key worry is that, with two years to talk about possible rules that might only be optional, the technology will race ahead, uncontrolled.
"We're likely to see the systems proliferate," said Anna Hehir, an expert in military AI governance at the Future of Life Institute. "They're not like nuclear weapons in that they're inaccessible. There are autonomous weapons that are easy to purchase or even to create for all kinds of actors: individuals, nonstate actors, criminal groups."
There are also big questions about how our existing rules of war – the Geneva Conventions – can be upheld if those doing the killing are not humans, but machines.
"These rules are the bare minimum that militaries and states have developed and agreed to adhere to," said the ICRC's Hinds. "The commander remains responsible for making sure that the use of force is lawful. The commander remains accountable. You cannot hold a machine accountable for a violation of the law."
How drones are reshaping modern warfare around the globe
But in the race to develop new weapons, no country wants to come second. Although most U.N. member states do agree there should be some controls over autonomous weapons, the compromise in Geneva means that, for the next two years at least, weapons that can use artificial intelligence to make life-and-death decisions will remain unregulated.
Meanwhile, weapons technology is developing at pace, while diplomacy is struggling to keep up.
